90ee1286527901e5: Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization.

The Germany-headquartered company, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update, Cleverbridge said it had cut off the intruders' access and launched an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems.
The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register, fills in some rather important blanks.

"Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers.
Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach.
More concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form.

Cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach.

Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk.

That doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems.

In its notification to customers, the company said it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion.

Affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase.
Two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®

2ccc08f42a138644: Tech companies are investing a lot of hope and money in rocks.

Google, Microsoft, and others have committed hundreds of millions of dollars to get startups to spread crushed basalt, olivine, or other alkaline materials across farms, in an effort to capture carbon from the air and lock it away. A number of influential models have found that this approach, known as enhanced rock weathering (ERW), could eventually remove 3 billion to 8 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, helping to slow or one day even reverse global warming. An additional promise is that these applications of rock could help farmers by improving the quality of their soil.

But a pair of preprint studies set for release today raise serious questions about how much material could be added to that soil before it may actually reduce the crop yields that are essential to farmers’ livelihoods, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report.

Cutting back on the rock applications to prevent these negative effects would shrink the method’s carbon dioxide removal capacity, likely capping it at less than a billion tons per year. The analyses were led by researchers at CarbonPlan, a San Francisco nonprofit known for rigorous scientific analysis of carbon removal methods.

These concerns come on top of a series of scientific questions about how to accurately estimate the carbon removal achieved through this approach and the possibility that some projects have overstated it, which researchers at CarbonPlan and elsewhere have raised in recent months and years.

“There’s still a heck of a lot we need to learn about ERW,” says Tyler Kukla, a research scientist at CarbonPlan and lead author of the new reports. “But a real tension, to me, exists between this massive amount of uncertainty and the big questions we have about whether or not this works, sitting alongside tremendous efforts to scale it up really quickly.”
How it works

There is no scientific dispute that certain rocks and minerals help to sequester carbon. Rain captures carbon dioxide molecules as it falls through the atmosphere, forming carbonic acid. When it lands on exposed silicate materials, that weak acid dissolves or chemically “weathers” the rocks.

The resulting calcium, magnesium, and carbon (in the form of bicarbonate) then travel on a long journey through creeks, streams, and rivers until they reach the ocean, where corals, mollusks, and other marine organisms may eventually use them to form calcium carbonate shells. As they die, those shells fall to the seafloor, combine with sediments, and form limestone rock that locks away the carbon.
If you thought that explanation was long, just imagine how long the process takes to unfold in real life! It’s not called the slow carbon cycle for nothing.

“Enhanced” rock weathering promises to accelerate the process. Grinding up the rocks and spreading them across fields creates much more surface area for carbonic acid to react with—and that should ultimately direct more carbon into the oceans.

ERW doesn’t require as much energy or infrastructure as other carbon dioxide removal options like direct-air-capture plants, and at least in the early rollout stages it can largely rely on waste material from rock mining operations.

But the big selling point is that there can be an economic benefit to doing it; it’s not just a cost like other forms of carbon removal. Added to agricultural soils, these sorts of rocks can increase nutrients, reduce acidity, and improve water retention, helping to boost crop yields (at least up to a point). Indeed, many farmers already routinely add crushed-up limestone to their soil to counteract the increased acidity caused by fertilizer use and other agricultural practices.
So carrying out enhanced rock weathering could merely be a matter of switching to other types of rock with the potential to lock away more carbon (about twice as much as limestone).
“It’s something the Earth has been doing for billions of years,” says Mary Yap, chief executive and cofounder of Lithos Carbon, an ERW startup. “It can scale. We know it works kinetically.”
“If we can figure out where in the world are the best places to do this and then make that happen,” she adds, “it can help both the communities and also help our atmosphere.”

Enhanced rock weathering could be of particular benefit to farmers who haven’t been able to manage their soil acidity, including many subsistence farmers in poorer parts of the world, says Tim Jesper Suhrhoff, a postdoctoral fellow at the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture. One recent study found that ERW boosted the median yields of smallholder farmers in India by more than 20%.
“That is huge for subsistence farmers,” he says.
Agricultural limits
But the new findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, suggest there could be a steep trade-off, at a certain point, between benefits for farmers and benefits for the climate.

A number of modeling studies that inform UN climate reports and national climate efforts have estimated that adding crushed rock to agricultural land could store away four to 12 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year (though some estimate lower levels). But the authors state in one of the new papers that these findings don’t account for the ways that significant levels of enhanced rock weathering will alter the pH of agricultural soil over time.

Initially it should merely reduce the soil acidity, but adding too much of these materials would eventually push up the pH beyond neutral and into alkaline territory. That could cause micronutrient deficiencies, disease susceptibility, and other problems for certain crops, potentially reducing yields—and, by extension, food supplies and farm revenue. That would likely force farmers to halt the practice, at least until soil pH returns to favorable levels.

The analysis found that preventing the more extreme effects of soil alkalization could limit ERW’s total potential to around 600 million tons of carbon dioxide removal per year, and even that may push pH levels too high for some crops, Kukla says. That’s a fraction of what some models have estimated.

“All of these models are assuming really, really optimistic things about what enhanced weathering can accomplish,” he says. “And when you just layer in the geochemistry that they’re missing, the numbers not only go down but get really uncertain.”
The researchers intend to submit the papers to peer-reviewed journals.
Rising popularity

Companies have been investing more and more money in ERW. In September, Google announced its largest carbon removal deal, as well as the biggest for this method to date: an agreement with the company Terradot to work with rice farmers in southern Brazil to apply enough crushed rock to their fields to draw down a million tons of carbon by 2040. (The deal includes a separate effort to cut methane emissions by draining the flooded paddies.) Google didn’t respond to an inquiry from MIT Technology Review.

Frontier, a coalition of companies that has committed to purchase $1.8 billion of carbon dioxide removal, has dedicated $121 million to prepurchasing 333,000 tons’ worth through enhanced rock weathering. That includes a $57 million deal with Lithos to remove more than 150,000 tons.
Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at Frontier, says the early data from their deals has demonstrated consistent weathering of rock across hundreds of fields.

He acknowledges there are remaining uncertainties, including how much of the carbon may be released before it’s permanently sequestered in the ocean. But he adds that those and other issues are all the subject of ongoing studies—including some Frontier has backed—by both ERW companies and academic groups.

All told, companies have committed to spending about $670 million on enhanced rock weathering to date, based on an average cost of about $350 per ton, according to CDR.fyi, a public-benefit corporation that provides independent data on the carbon removal sector. A working group of the UN’s climate panel, the European Commission, and other government agencies are also in discussions about the possibility of incorporating ERW into national or regional climate efforts.
Tempered expectations

The new papers add to a growing recognition that enhanced rock weathering is more constrained and “more complicated than we initially thought,” says Rebecca Neumann, who leads a hydro-biogeochemistry research group at the University of Washington but was not involved in the studies.

In April, researchers at CarbonPlan, the nonprofit that led the new studies, raised concerns about an allotment of carbon credits that Lithos received for this method. The startup claimed to have removed 8.3 tons of carbon dioxide per hectare per year through ERW, but the CarbonPlan team noted that this figure exceeds around 90% of the rates reported in previously published experiments.

CarbonPlan followed up on that report the following month with an analysis finding that modeling of enhanced weathering has often relied on an equation that could inflate the surface area of the crushed rock—and, in turn, overstate the amount of carbon dioxide removal achieved.

Finally, several studies last year highlighted a known but important issue: Magnesium and calcium ions can get trapped in soil for long periods instead of traveling with the bicarbonate into the oceans. That creates a risk that the bicarbonate will simply dissolve back into carbon dioxide and water again, “resulting in no carbon removed,” explained Robert Höglund, cofounder of CDR.fyi, in an online post. Or it may delay the carbon removal by years to decades.
“I’m not saying it doesn’t work,” Höglund said in an interview. “I’m pointing out there’s a lot of uncertainty about what’s permanent and how we should measure it.”

Lithos’s Yap stresses that the high rate of carbon removal the company reported in that instance simply reflected large applications of more finely crushed rock on farms with favorable soil chemistry, adding that the project applied as much as 10 times more per hectare than some of the studies cited in the CarbonPlan post. She also criticized the nonprofit for not contacting the company before posting its results and for publishing them on a blog instead of in peer-reviewed literature.
Kukla says CarbonPlan did account for higher applications of crushed rock in its analysis.

A few additional findings further underscore the complexity and uncertainty surrounding this approach. For example, a more recent preprint suggests that the equation CarbonPlan critiqued does accurately capture the rock surface area in some cases. Meanwhile, other papers have found that the problem of trapped calcium and magnesium ions could be mitigated through location choices and certain land management practices.
Healthy debate
But all this back and forth raises an obvious question: how can commercial deployments of this practice proceed while the scientific debate is still unfolding?

Kevin Sutherland, a carbon removal scientist at Isometric, one of the first carbon registries to develop methods for certifying how much carbon a project draws out of the atmosphere, says the company accounts for these scientific uncertainties by quantifying the climate benefits of ERW conservatively.

“In practice, this means projects receive fewer certificates than our best estimate of the carbon they remove,” he explained in an emailed response. “We would always rather issue too few certificates than too many.”
Despite the recent findings, Neumann says that ERW is still a promising approach for helping farmers and the climate, even if the carbon removal potential is significantly lower than initially hoped.

Yale’s Suhrhoff, who also read over the new findings but was not involved in the research, says that providing a clearer sense of ideal application levels can help the approach catch on. “If we figure out where enhanced rock weathering makes sense agronomically and how much enhanced rock weathering to do to reach agronomic optimal conditions, I think this can actually greatly improve the realistic uptake speed of this technology,” he says.
Kukla himself stresses that none of CarbonPlan’s research suggests enhanced rock weathering doesn’t work or can’t make a meaningful contribution to slowing down climate change.

But it’s important to understand the potential scale, he adds, because the world needs to know how much we can count on any given form of carbon removal—and how hard we’ll need to pull on other climate levers, including the basic job of cutting greenhouse-gas emissions.
“This is all just about calibrating our expectations and grounding them in the science as best as we can,” he says.

452ad0518845baf4: Xfce's next release is taking shape for 2027, while MATE users have fresh options for moving their familiar desktop onto Wayland.

One of the oldest surviving Linux desktops has a relatively slow release schedule: new stable releases of Xfce tend to appear every two years. The project just updated its release engineering roadmap for the forthcoming Xfce 4.22, and it looks like the next version won't arrive until early next year.

We covered the release of Xfce 4.20 in December 2024, but 4.22 is still incubating. The roadmap schedules its first prerelease and feature freeze for December 15, 2026, followed by a second prerelease on January 15, 2027. A third prerelease is optional, and neither that nor the final release has a date. February or March might be plausible, but that's our guess, not the project's promise. The Xfce developers tend not to rush into things.

Wayland development continues in 4.22, building on the preliminary support in 4.20. The team is also working on its own compositor, xfwl4, although the roadmap doesn't promise feature parity with X11. (In Wayland terminology, the "compositor" is the combined display server and window manager.) The compositor has its own development roadmap. The name is a nod to the current Xfce X11 window manager, which is called xfwm4.

The main developer of the new xfwl4 compositor is Brian Tarricone, who has been working on other parts of Xfce since 2004. Back in July, he shared a blog post about his use of generative-AI coding assistants called LLMs and xfwl4.

He says: "So yes, I use Claude quite a bit while developing xfwl4. I don't vibe-code, ever, and I probably use the LLM to generate less code than most people do. After all, building things with code is my hobby and passion (and I'm lucky I got to do it professionally for a quarter century), and driving an LLM is kinda boring."

We find this somewhat reassuring, but any really passionate anti-LLM Xfce users reading this may be glad that the release schedules of Ubuntu LTS versions and Xfce stable releases are so far out of sync – sticking with Xubuntu 26.04 means there's no immediate need to adopt the new LLM-assisted compositor. Or, of course, simply keep using X11 instead of Wayland – although that might eventually mean choosing a distro that maintains X11 support, perhaps through XLibre, which has other drawbacks for some.

There are other options, too. We've also seen an independent fork of xfwm4 called xfwm4-gl. It's in active development and uses OpenGL to perform window compositing directly, while the current version uses the now rather old Xrender extension.
Labwc and MATE Wayland, and Wayfire, and Polo too

Last year, when we looked at the release candidate of openSUSE Leap 16.0, we found that it ran Xfce on Wayland by replacing Xfwm4 with the labwc compositor that we first saw in PiOS 5.2. This worked well – about the only difference we could find was the absence of some window-management shortcuts.

(Saying that, this vulture is still happy with X11. There is only one Wayland feature we want: the ability to set different dots-per-inch ratios on different screens. We can approximate that on X11 by scaling individual outputs. This works well enough – it just makes one of the screens look a little fuzzy.)

Labwc is one of the more flexible, and X11-like, compositors out there, and can be found in other projects. Scott Sturrock recently wrote to us to tell us about his new MATE Wayland Desktop project. This is an independent distro, combining an Ubuntu 26.04 base, the latest MATE 1.29, and version 0.9 of the labwc compositor. (That's from labwc's older 0.9 series; the latest release is 0.20.3. The numbering jumped to align with the version of wlroots it uses, while 0.9 remains a maintenance branch.)

MATE is a continuing fork of GNOME 2.32, the final release of GNOME 2. GNOME 2 used the Metacity X11 window manager – indeed, the Windows-like GNOME Flashback session still uses Metacity, which is currently at version 3.56.0. MATE's fork of Metacity is called Marco.

There is already a way to run MATE using Wayland: the MATE Wayland Session uses the Wayfire compositor. Wayfire was inspired by Compiz, the 3D compositing window manager remembered for its "wobbly windows" effect, and Wayfire has lots of its own special effects, as the Wayfire wiki's tutorial demonstrates with a lot of animated images. Wayfire is quite a capable environment in its own right – so, arguably, somewhat overkill for the traditional-style MATE environment.

As yet another alternative, developer Kerem Söke recently announced a new MATE-specific compositor called Polo. Polo is intended as a direct replacement for Marco. The Polo 1.0 release notes tell some of the story. Polo aims to be as similar as it can to the familiar Marco window manager: it picks up existing configuration, keystrokes, Alt-Tab behaviour, and so on. It's already at version 1.0.2. It can do wobbly windows and so on as well, it has its own polo-tweaks program, and a roadmap for improving MATE's integration with Wayland.

Both projects went public around the same time, but MATE Wayland Desktop is already packaged up and ready to install. We suspect that if Polo is successful, it will find its way into the Ubuntu repositories, and perhaps the two projects will eventually come together.
Xfce is about a year older than KDE – however, the early releases of Xfce weren't open source. So, KDE is the oldest Linux desktop that has been open source from the start.

Xfce isn't the oldest Linux desktop of all, though. There were some proprietary commercial desktop environments around before either Xfce or KDE existed, such as IXI's X.desktop [PDF]. Most originally ran on commercial Unixes and were later ported to Linux – but they didn't stick around into the modern FOSS era. ®
bf861a7a15dd0ad6: BRUSSELS: Business activity in the euro area registered a "steady" expansion this month, a key survey showed Monday, as faster growth in Germany helped counter a deepening downturn in France.

"While growth in Germany has accelerated to the fastest for four and a half years, as its manufacturing sector enjoys a growth spurt of the likes not seen for over five years, France is suffering a deepening downturn," Williamson said.
The German economy, he said, was benefiting strongly from "surging investment spending on defence and AI-related technologies".

At the same time, "uncertainty about the political environment, social unrest and the high cost of living are hitting service providers especially hard, especially for consumer-facing businesses, dampening growth both in France and across the rest of the region as a whole".

The European Central Bank has lifted borrowing costs twice this year in response to the energy shock triggered by the US war on Iran, and Williamson warned that "higher interest rates are also starting to show up as an increasing drag".
He noted that lower oil prices had "helped tame inflationary pressures" somewhat in November.
But he predicted the PMI data alongside a "broad message" of eurozone growth would bolster calls for a further rate increase in December.

b8f3f1036ed781fe: Airbus has a plan to phase out Microsoft Office, but about 22 percent of its roughly 165,000 employees will stay on it because their sensitive data must remain on-premise.

In March 2018, Airbus signed a contract with Google to move its workforce - 130,000 strong at that time - onto the cloud-based Workspace suite. Years later, compatibility issues mean some users still need Excel.
Catherine Jestin, Airbus's executive vice president of digital, told The Register that Google is still working to resolve software interface conflicts between departments and improve features.

Last year, for example, Google tripled the number of cells available in Sheets, which let Airbus "reduce significantly the number of users on Microsoft." This year, Google improved the compatibility of document watermarking. Contracts, for instance, are often exported from Excel to Sheets by one department, edited by another, and sent back.
"Sometimes we had compatibility issues when you were commenting, the comments were lost, or they were not transferable in one way or the other," she said.

"Now they [Google] have made it totally compatible, which means that it makes it much easier for us to decommission people working on contracts… the legal department, the sales department, purchasing department, making it much easier to have that internal collaboration."
Airbus and Google have a roadmap to eliminate Microsoft Office. Jestin expects the migration to finish in "another two to three years."
Not every part of the company will switch. The Defence division, which accounts for the 22 percent (more than 36,000 people), will keep using classic Microsoft Office.

"We will not get 100 percent out of Microsoft because again, for the defense industry people, they cannot [use] Microsoft Office 365 or Google Workspace, they have to stay on-premise, and the only solution that is available on-premise is Microsoft. fe06cd745c7bca00: PARIS: French president Emmanuel Macron has proposed reviving a 2011 proposal to enshrine a framework for public finances in the constitution, as a possible response to concerns in financial markets over France's fiscal trajectory.

The draft constitutional reform, endorsed by parliament in 2011 but never fully enacted, would have created binding, multi-year framework laws for public finances.

Annual targets would be set for public spending, revenue and the budget balance over a period of at least three years, with the constitutional court empowered to strike down legislation that breached the rules.
Macron said a debate over reviving the proposal was "not illegitimate", while stressing that the government was closely watching borrowing costs and the spread between French and German bond yields.
The move appears aimed at reassuring investors at a time when bond markets have been fretting over France's public finances.
France's public debt stands at around 119% of GDP, while uncertainty surrounds the 2027 budget ahead of a presidential race to succeed Macron.

The 2011 proposal was endorsed by both houses of parliament. To become part of the constitution it would require further approval, either by a referendum or by a three-fifths majority of lawmakers meeting in a joint session of parliament, known as Congress.
Several political forces have already voiced support for the principle, including Macron's allies, the mainstream right and the far-right National Rally (RN).

RN leader Marine Le Pen, a presidential frontrunner, said on Sunday that her party had itself called for such a measure and would be inclined to back it, although she suggested the 2011 text was not as strong as a version favoured by her party.
The support of the RN could prove decisive, as parties on the left have criticised the proposal as an excessive constraint on future governments' economic policy choices.

Among the many organizations to adopt Outage As A Service (OAAS) were Microsoft, Apple, the FAA, and any number of European supermarkets. Even the NSA has succumbed. For us, at least, outage is word of the year. It's certainly deeply embedded in the public mind, with schoolchildren reportedly referring to the 19th century Irish famine as "the potato outage." There's no danger of an outrage outage.

OAAS is synonymous with infrastructure failure, a more useful term that begins to hint at cause and cure as well as effect. In all of the latest crop, what we know is depressingly familiar. Microsoft's O365 meltdown was a cascading failure caused by a botched upgrade that took stuff offline and melted down as it tried to come back. The FAA was a migration from Jurassic hardware that wasn't end of life so much as living fossil. The Eurofridge-cum-fondue-maker was a control system so badly written it fell apart if you raised an eyebrow at it. Clearly, nobody had. Until now.

These are all different classes of OAAS that have been around for decades. Security-based outages are still outages, and a packet flood is still a packet flood whether it's a botnet DDoS or finger trouble in the config dashboard.

Each of them has a root cause with obvious fixes – a faulty mental model of network/server interaction, chronic underfunding, a complete supply chain with little cyber-security expertise. All these, like the poor, will be with us always. They won't fix themselves. Infrastructure that works is invisible, and invisible things are forgotten until they break. What's needed is an infrastructure that watches itself, that is designed to be adaptive and resilient, one that refuses to connect to danger and nulls out any that gets through.

There have been attempts to create a ground-up architecture that is inherently risk resistant. One such is SCION (Scalability, Control, and Isolation On Next-generation networks). It redesigns routing between domains around explicit path selection, separate control and data planes, and mechanisms for trust and failure isolation. The result is a very resilient, very reliable, and very secure infrastructure that reflects the designers' tenet that you can't patch the internet into any of these things. Start from scratch or GTFO.

SCION started about 15 years ago, and it works well enough to be adopted by entities like the Secure Swiss Finance Network. If the Gnomes of Zurich trust it, no higher accreditation exists. Well, it was designed by ETH Zürich. Where you won't find it is almost everywhere else. The internet is like Switzerland in the same way the Amazon rainforest is like Central Park. There are trees and sometimes it rains. It is unwise to infer anything else.

Given you can't manicure existing infrastructure into true resilience, the only other option is evolution. A couple of billion years of continued life on Earth has proved this is the only way to re-engineer complex systems while they're usefully running. In this case, the current evolutionary endpoint that's of most interest is the human immune system.

An interlocking system of functions, it takes care of uncountably thousands of pathogen-based threats and internal malfunctions every day. You might think that the 30-odd billion computing machines making up today's Internet are impossible to monitor and secure, but that's peanuts to the human immune system. An average human has around 30 trillion cells, and roughly the same again in bacteria. When it works, the mechanics of the human infrastructure are invisible and out of mind. The immune system makes it so, and everything involved is driven by information, signaling and behavior. There is pattern matching, resource management, defense in depth and reinforcement learning in persistent models. Sounds familiar?

The analogy between this and modern digital infrastructure is so irresistible that it has been around for a lifetime. Viruses, infections, swarms, worms, system health are so familiar that they go unremarked. The term Digital Immune System has been around since the last century too, pushed by outfits like IBM, Symantec and Gartner. It hasn't taken off, probably because it's been marketing bunkum instead of describing the development of inherently resilient infrastructure based on insights from biology.

It has also been true that natural selection, the engine of evolution and this biology, only works in IT at the most macro, capitalist level of product and company survival. Everything else is selected through design decisions, market analysis, and insight versus delusion. The adoption of immunological concepts to digital infrastructure will have to be the result of rigorous exploration of complex systems and cross-disciplinary research. What would that look like?

There are academics thinking just these thoughts: see this paper [PDF] from Kay Smarsly at Technische Universität Hamburg. Like SCION, it takes an architectural look at what resiliency might look like, but with explicit reference to biological systems.

OAAS is a chronic syndrome with multiple causes and potentially fatal outcomes. It exists and persists because digital infrastructure too often fails to contain internal failures or external attacks. We have a working example of an approach to managing analogous problems in systems far vaster and more intricate than any we have built. We now have tools that may start to do systemic analysis and inference at a useful scale. In an industry prepared to bet billions on agents that do your shopping, there is every reason to kick off serious research into digital immune systems worthy of the name. Doctor, cure thyself. ®

27d7ef6284c935a9: Humanity’s third-ever mission to Mercury has arrived, but a last-minute “software issue” has complicated matters.

The BepiColombo mission is a joint effort by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Reaching Mercury is not easy because its gravity is weak and its orbit is fast. The tiny planet’s proximity to the Sun further complicates matters, because our star’s gravity accelerates everything that falls towards it.

BepiColombo’s journey has therefore seen it whiz past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times on a complicated path the two space agencies designed to slow it down sufficiently to be captured by mercurial gravity, while also keeping up with its rapid orbit.
In 2024, the craft’s thrusters underperformed, leading the ESA and JAXA to re-plot the planned trajectory and reschedule its arrival at Mercury from mid-2025 to this past weekend.

The ESA’s operations team sent the commands to insert BepiColombo into orbit on Friday. On Sunday the craft phoned home with news that it entered orbit. A little later, however, the ESA revealed “the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software issue.”
The spacecraft is safe, but the ESA says it is “working to understand what happened” and promised updates early this week.
Readers may recall that a pair of NASA missions to Mars are also experiencing software glitches, which have in recent weeks become all-too-prevalent on Earth, too.
If all is well, BepiColombo will deploy two orbiters.

The ESA’s craft is called the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which the ESA says will map the planet, assess the composition of its surface and interior, measure its magnetic field, and even gather data that scientists hope will “test Einstein's theory of General Relativity to an unprecedented level of accuracy.”
JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MIO) will also investigate the planet’s magnetic field, plasma, dust, and atmosphere.

Both orbiters are extraordinary feats of engineering. As JAXA explains, MIO is solar-powered but the sunlight it will receive at Mercury is around ten times as powerful as on Earth. Mercury itself is also sufficiently hot that the orbiter needs protection from heat radiated from the planet’s surface. ESA’s MPO keeps itself cool with three to four insulating blankets comprised of layered titanium, aluminum, and a ceramic fabric called Nextel. The blankets alone weigh 94kg.
The two space agencies expect to start science operations in April 2027 but haven’t yet said if the two orbiters are in peak condition.

JAXA, sadly, last week revealed that its Hayabusa2 probe has deteriorated to the point at which it can no longer make its planned landing on asteroid 1998 KY26. JAXA scheduled that for the year 2031, but problems with the probe’s thrusters mean the agency will instead attempt a high-speed fly-by of asteroid 2015 BM510 in 2028. Hayabusa2 launched in 2014, so is rather older than BepiColombo.

Humanity has visited Mercury twice before. Mariner 10 made three rapid passes across 1974 and 1975, when it managed to map less than half of the planet’s surface. Messenger made it to Mercury in 2011 and spent more than four years in orbit before crashing into the planet’s surface. The probe mapped the entire planet and even spotted ice near its poles. ®

cb733f0aea6c2643: Women in Niger face barriers accessing their rights in disputes over land, inheritance, and child custody
Originally published on Global Voices
Nigerien women gathered at an awareness-raising session on the fight against jihadism. Screenshot via France 24's YouTube channel. Fair use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In 2024, Niger had a population of over 27 million. However, according to the Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey (eJNS) conducted by the Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) and the Ministry of Justice, more than half experienced justice problems that year.

Overall, 61 percent of the population has experienced at least one issue accessing justice. And while men are more likely to report these problems (70 percent) than women (52 percent), this does not in any way mean women suffer fewer injustices. Instead, it underscores the fact that many women either do not recognize their challenges as justice problems or do not advocate for themselves. The survey results therefore indicate that while women need justice just as much as men, they face greater obstacles in obtaining it.

Long before reaching any courtroom, women face barriers not only within their families and communities, but also in the resolution of disputes, often over land, inheritance, and child custody. This survey also shows how the outcome of a dispute can ultimately shape a woman’s income, economic security, and ability to invest in her future.
Invisible problems

Within Niger, the gap between men and women’s rights is obvious. As 41 percent of women say they are unaware of their legal rights, women (38 percent) are more likely than men (34 percent) to drop an ongoing court case. What’s more, almost two-thirds (64 percent) of women also have no formal education, compared to 47 percent of men.

Domestic violence (DV) is the most pressing issue faced by women in Niger, far surpassing crime, neighbor conflicts, and land disputes, with 29 percent saying they have experienced some kind of intimate partner violence. Between 2022 and 2024, domestic violence jumped from the eighth most serious problem for the general population to the third. According to HiiL, this may signal a shift in attitude toward reporting such incidents.

Across different datasets, land disputes over field boundaries, inheritance, contested sales, and crop damage rank second (17 percent) behind crime (23 percent) among the most serious justice problems. In its October 2026 report, HiiL also found that land problems accounted for 23 percent of all recorded justice problems, with a severity score of 7.1.

For women in rural areas, where more than 80 percent of Nigeriens currently live, land provides food, income, and economic autonomy. However, traditional practices, family pressures, and systems where people farm land they do not own keep their access uncertain. HiiL thereby conducted a qualitative study in the Dosso and Tillabéri regions, ultimately producing a best-practice manual for justice practitioners.
Inheritance: A silent injustice

Nigerien statutory law grants women the right to own, use, and inherit land. However, in practice, customary and family rules often deny them what is rightfully theirs. In some areas, once married, women are thought to belong to their husbands’ families, precluding them from inheriting land from their birth families.

In its 2025 Annual Report, HiiL shares real-life stories, such as Saouda’s, exemplifying this reality. Widow and mother of five, Saouda lost access to her late husband’s land when his relatives claimed ownership, but successfully regained it after learning about her rights through an awareness-raising campaign.

This exclusion has a direct economic impact on those women. They not only lose inherited land, but also a source of income, food security, and the ability to invest in livestock, trade, or farm improvements.
Child custody

After a separation, divorce, or the death of a partner, family-made agreements often determine where the children live, who provides for them, and whether their mother can maintain a meaningful relationship with them. These decisions are often made out of court, where customary norms hold considerable sway.

In its report, HiiL highlighted this issue through Amina’s story. Detained following a custody battle over her children, Amina thought her only hope was her family. After being told she could not legally win custody after a divorce under Islam, she had no idea she had such rights.
In this region, customary rulings tend to favor male authority in family matters, with customary chiefs typically awarding custody to fathers on religious grounds.

In 2020, the General Report of the National Consultation on Justice found that women were underrepresented in the judiciary, accounting for just 39 of the 399 magistrates in late 2017. Although customary court hearings may be more welcoming for women, no women sit among the customary assessors, prompting the report to recommend their inclusion.
The social norm burden

For almost a third of women, preserving family relations is the main reason they do not turn to courts or customary authorities. Any woman who claims her share of inheritance or custody of her children could be seen as “causing problems” or dividing her family. Consequently, testimonies gathered across the country tell stories of women fearing they will damage their families’ honor and relatives advising them to stay silent, at the expense of their rights.

Economic constraints only add to their difficulties. Due to insufficient funds, about four percent of women say they did not take action even when they knew their rights were being violated. Financial dependence on their partner or family also limits their ability to pursue legal proceedings. Quoting an NGO official, HiiL shared:
Les femmes viennent souvent nous voir après avoir épuisé leurs maigres ressources. Elles sont alors coincées, incapables de poursuivre leurs quêtes de recherche de solution à leurs problèmes.
Caught in a bind and unable to pursue their search for solutions, women often come to us after exhausting their already limited resources.

About a quarter of women with justice problems choose not to act, believing that legal action will not lead to a fair outcome. Zara, a 25-year-old Nigerien woman unable to afford legal fees and forced to drop a domestic violence case, stated:

Même si je préfère aller devant le juge je ne pourrai pas car je n’ai pas les moyens. Je ne suis qu’une vendeuse d’eau fraîche et de Bissap, même si je sais que je peux aller devant le juge si mon mari ne me nourrit pas, je n’ai pas de quoi supporter les aller-retours et autres frais qu’on demande à la justice.

Even though I would prefer to take my case to court, I can’t afford it. I only sell chilled water and bissap [herbal drink]. While I may be entitled to go to court if my husband didn’t support me, I couldn’t afford the round trips and other legal fees.

Even when women know about their rights, they still tend to choose customary justice over formal justice. Although it is often biased and patriarchal, it is also faster, closer to home, and delivered in their native language. As such, 40 percent of women identify family as a source of support, compared to just 28 percent of men. Meanwhile, only four percent of women and six percent of men turn to formal courts.

According to data published in the daily newspaper Le Sahel in 2024, men (75 percent) take legal action more often than women (71 percent). While this gap may be modest, it nonetheless compounds other obstacles.
Solutions exist

Typically, Nigerians will seek out informal pathways to settle disputes. In the 2024 Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey, direct negotiation (40 percent), family (33 percent), and customary or traditional authorities (24 percent) were the most commonly cited sources of help, far surpassing formal courts (five percent). HiiL subsequently recommended including these actors in the justice process by conferring full legal status on customary decisions or strengthening mediation and conciliation pathways.

Established under Law No. 2011-42, the National Agency for Legal and Judicial Assistance (ANAJJ) provides free consultations, information on rights, guidance, and legal aid for those in financial need. According to the 2025 statistics, 33,394 beneficiaries received legal assistance, including 8,489 women. Meanwhile, its regional offices awarded 3,747 legal aid grants, including 550 to women.

In December 2025, during the first National Week of Legal and Judicial Assistance for women and children, Minister of Justice Alio Daouda presented different figures. Such discrepancies — at odds with independent NGO and journalistic findings — mean that official administrative reports must be read with caution.

The ANAJJ covers all of the country’s eight regions, but leaves many rural areas underserved. That said, additional initiatives do exist, including those led by the Association of Women Lawyers of Niger, an organization that has offered women and children legal assistance for 35 years.

However, resolution remains a stumbling block. According to the 2024 Justice Needs and Satisfaction survey, 56 percent of justice problems remain unresolved, with 20 percent on hold and 36 percent dropped. Conversely, 72 percent of solutions achieved are considered fair. While taking action significantly improves the chance of resolution, the main challenge is no longer just access itself, but seeing cases through to their conclusion.
Justice for women

The issue is not just the existence of courts, but ensuring women know they have rights, understand how to enforce them, and can do so without fear of rejection from their family or community. Awareness of their rights should go hand in hand with the ability to exercise them and the support of religious and traditional leaders alike.

In rural areas, practical steps are being taken to make this a reality. Traditional, female, and religious leaders have all received training in women’s land rights. After a female leader called for access to a plot of land for her group, the village chief publicly committed to finding one. Radio and theater, in local languages, have also enabled some women to claim their rights. According to HiiL, the objective is not only to recognize their rights in legislation, but to create practical conditions for exercising them.

Achieving justice that truly meets Nigerien women’s needs requires several steps: legal information in local languages, legal clinics in rural areas, training for traditional and religious authorities, protection for women’s inheritance, support in land and family disputes, and the inclusion of women among customary assessors.

As long as land, inheritance, and child custody decisions are made behind closed doors, with no guarantee of fairness, a considerable number of Nigerien women will continue to lose not only their assets but also a significant proportion of their economic independence.
Written (Français) by Jean Sovon
Translated (English) by Laura

7aaf06ba478f7615: Returning to work after the weekend can feel like voluntarily walking into a trap. To help readers feel a little freer, The Register therefore uses Monday mornings to serve up a new installment of "Who, Me?" It's the column in which we share your stories of mistakes, misjudgments, and occasional misanthropy.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Marshall," who told us about a job interview he endured about 20 years ago.
The interview included a practical component he described as "Here's a PC, we've broken a few things in it, get it going."
Marshall quickly spotted some mundane faults, such as a loose PCI card and unplugged internal cables.
He felt the test was too easy. "One of the things I always checked was whether the power supply 110/230 switch was set for the UK," he told The Register.
Getting the PC running earned Marshall a job offer, but he couldn't resist suggesting a tougher test.
"I said to my future manager: 'Would it be a good thing to set the power supply to the wrong voltage as part of the interview test?' He said that wasn't fair."
Marshall stayed in the job for two years. A couple of months after he left, his former manager sent him a short email.
Marshall asked another former colleague what might have prompted that email.
"It turned out somebody – I don't know if it was an interview candidate – had blown a power supply by not checking the voltage it was set to."
What a coincidence! Or maybe not?
"It wasn't anything to do with me," Marshall insisted. "No idea who it was."

Have you held colleagues to a higher standard than the boss expected? Or left a little trap for them to trip over? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? 315fb775dc30231e: A new technique developed by MIT researchers could help engineers use artificial intelligence to streamline the design and innovation of analog integrated circuits, semiconductor chips that perform vital functions like communication and power management in electronic devices. In the future, this method could allow engineers to prototype faster, explore a wider range of chip designs, and discover new design schemes that might improve the performance and energy efficiency of robots, medical monitors, or industrial sensors. Designing analog integrated circuits that meet specific requirements is usually a cumbersome manual process due to the enormous number of possibilities. Frontier generative AI models have shown success in automating the process, but using these resource-intensive, cloud-hosted models could expose proprietary circuit design and semiconductor foundry data to malicious users. The MIT method, called Small LM Iterating on Circuits, or SLIC (pronounced “slick”), enables engineers to train a small language model to perform analog circuit design as well as or better than a frontier large language model (LLM).  This small model is inexpensive and efficient enough to run on a laptop. Because it’s trained and deployed locally, it can use a company’s circuit design data without raising privacy risks.  When compared to complementary baselines and open-weight frontier LLMs, a small model trained by SLIC more effectively generated designs that achieved the circuit objectives.  “We’ve provided an alternative option to automate analog circuit design. With our technique, engineers can train a small, locally deployable model, using their own confidential data, and then deploy it in their own environment to ensure their assets remain protected,” says Yan Xu, an electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) graduate student and lead author of a paper on this technique. She is joined on the paper by senior author Ruonan Han, a professor of EECS and a member of the MIT Research Laboratory of Electronics; Zhengqi Gao PhD ’26; Wenjie Lu PhD ’18, a former MIT postdoc who is now a principal research scientist at Analog Devices, Inc.; Xin Zhang, a research manager at IBM Research; Duane S. Boning, the Clarence J. LeBel Professor in EECS and MIT vice provost for international activities; and others at IBM Research and Analog Devices. The research will be presented at the 2026 Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems.  “Through some specialized training and area-specific research, we can use much smaller models that consume far fewer resources to achieve almost the same results as flagship models in analog circuit design,” says Han. “This opens many more possibilities in the design of complex chips, especially if we care about costs, data privacy, and customization.” Mimicking human learning Analog integrated circuits enable a device to interact with the physical world. For instance, these circuits boost incoming wireless signals in smartphones and process outputs from sensors that track a car’s engine temperature.  Real-world signals tend to be unpredictable, so engineers must balance a wide and complex array of targets and tradeoffs to maximize analog circuit performance. This has made the design problem especially challenging for AI models. “To design a circuit, engineers find a good starting point based on their intuition and then, drawing on their knowledge of circuit design, tune a few knobs toward the performance they want,” says Xu. “There is no universal way to solve every circuit design problem.” Even if a powerful, cloud-based model could design a circuit as well as a human, most companies would be reluctant to send their foundry-specific data to external AI service providers. With SLIC, the MIT researchers created a training method that teaches a smaller, less expensive, faster language model to design analog integrated circuits that meet user specifications.  The SLIC model uses a few billion parameters, making it several thousand times smaller than frontier models that use trillions of parameters and require enormous amounts of computational resources.  “We tried to mimic the behavior of how a human learns to design a circuit,” Xu says. They used a technique called multi-turn reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where a model works through a multi-step task while adapting to environmental feedback.  When given an analog circuit optimization task, SLIC uses a large LLM to generate several demonstrations of the open source design process. Then SLIC then uses these demonstrations to guide the small model in mimicking this design process.  After the small model gains some initial knowledge about circuit design, SLIC lets it practice by tackling a new design problem on its own. The model makes an initial guess of the design parameters, performs simulations, evaluates the results, and iteratively refines the design using knowledge it gained about analog circuits. Once a design achieves the user’s goals, SLIC prioritizes additional marginal gains. This means the model keeps learning to make improvements that boost performance even when several designs meet the user-defined targets.  An interpretable process Importantly, because SLIC employs models that describe their reasoning using natural language, the user can understand the decisions it makes along the way. “Although the whole process is automated, the user can see what is going on inside the model. This could help the user gain some new ideas about circuit design, and it also adds a lot of confidence about the decision-making process,” Han says. An engineer could utilize SLIC by adapting the researchers’ trained model to their data using a fine-tuning process. Or they could employ the SLIC training process to build their own model with company data, allowing for more customization. “We are seeing an increasing demand for analog chips, but the speed of design has not kept up. This research is trying to bring new capabilities to AI to solve a problem that industry has been stuck on for decades,” Lu says. When the researchers tested SLIC’s ability to design a circuit that met desired performance metrics, their small model came close to matching the performance of the latest GPT model (GPT-6-Astra). It did this while using a fraction of the computational resources.  The researchers also found that the SLIC model maintained its performance when tackling previously unseen circuit structures and adapting to more advanced technology nodes (design and manufacturing rules) and real commercial processes. Because SLIC teaches a model the general chip design process, the system is not tied to any company. This makes it a more scalable approach that could be used by many organizations for a range of circuit applications. “The knowledge the model has gained about circuit design is universal in nature. That is the powerful aspect of this tool,” Han says. In the future, the researchers want to explore self-improving models that can independently learn to handle more diverse topologies and design targets. They also want to use SLIC to build a multi-agent framework, in which many small language models work on different parts of a complex circuit design task. “Yan’s work shows that a locally deployable model can learn transferable design behavior and iterate with a circuit simulator to improve a design, which could reduce repetitive manual tuning for engineers. This is the kind of work the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab makes possible. We see it as opening the door to more sophisticated custom design, including RF and microwave circuits, in the settings where industry actually works,” says Zhang. This research is funded, in part, by Analog Device, Inc., IBM, and the John L. Ocampo Endowment Fund of MACOM Technology Solutions.
8032565a25b5764d: Google’s Mandiant unit has claimed that the critical flaw VMware last week revealed in its vCenter product was under attack by a China-linked threat actor which knew of the bug in July and exploited it in September.
VMware revealed several flaws on November 19. The big nasty is CVE-2026-123890, which allows unauthorized access to vCenter, the management console for hosts and guest VMs.

According to seven researchers from Google’s threat intelligence group (formerly Mandiant), a crew it calls ARMORY CASTLE that it suspects of having links to the People’s Republic of China exploited CVE-2026-123890 by first compromising remote access appliances from BeyondTrust.
Google’s analysis suggests the crew uses that toehold to establish access to other Linux appliances before moving deeper into victims’ networks.

If the crew finds vCenter, it deploys a custom malware tool called “BONESAW” designed to slice into the VMware product. In the incident Google observed, BONESAW let attackers “forge authentication tokens, bypass MFA, and impersonate any user.”

The gang put that access to work by conducting an inventory of the victim’s VMware setup, scooping up data describing the ESXi file system, attached disks, and mounted Virtual Machine File System volumes. ARMORY CASTLE also added an SSH public key to the root account’s authorized keys, and “conducted further reconnaissance and data theft on the ESXi filesystem using the root account.”
Google also found evidence of BONESAW being used in July, on a server an unidentified entity had patched against CVE-2026-59309 – another authentication bypass vulnerability in vCenter.

And BONESAW was just one of five tools Google thinks ARMORY CASTLE created as part of its plan to attack vCenter. It also made webshells named SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, a backdoor called BEARBONES, and a SAML utility called SAWSNAKE.

“The use of three separate specialized sets of malware and two zero-days in the course of a single campaign indicates that there are significant resources supporting ARMORY CASTLE operations,” Google’s researchers wrote. “It also shows the extent of the threat actor’s operational commitment to compromise high priority targets.”
Few targets are as juicy as vCenter, because it can literally give attackers access to thousands of virtual machines and the hosts they run on.
Google hasn't said how many attacks is saw on vCenter using BONESAW.

The Register asked VMware if it was aware of the September attack, if it took any measures to defend its customers at the time, and to share a timeline for disclosure and remediation of CVE-2026-123890.

A spokesperson responded by pointing to VMware’s Q&A document and stating “In today's threat environment, customers should assume any publicly disclosed critical vulnerability can and will be exploited by threat actors under the right conditions and should apply the recommended patches immediately.”

VMware has tried to make that easier by adding non-disruptive patching to several of its products, and introducing a product called vDefend that offers “virtual patching” by creating compensating controls that use network micro segmentation and other techniques to block access to resources malware uses. Last month, VMware debuted another new tool, HyperArmor, to block incoming malicious traffic targeting its VCF private cloud suite.
In recent discussions with The Register, VMware execs told us the Broadcom business unit will emphasize security improvements in future product releases.

“Our teams have integrated frontier AI security model testing directly into our engineering workflows, strengthened our software supply chain to reduce third-party dependencies and speed up upstream responses, and built VCF 9.1 specifically for high-velocity security,” a spokesperson said in response to questions about the Mandiant report.
Freebie patches hard to find

One security offering VMware won’t continue is free access to patches for zero-day flaws in supported versions of products sold under its old perpetual licenses – even to users who don’t have an ongoing support deal or software subscription.
VMware last year stopped making those patches available for download and promised it would establish “a separate patch delivery cycle.”

Readers have pointed out that information about the new cycle isn’t easy to find, and The Register noticed that the blog post in which Broadcom CEO Hock Tan promised the free patches no longer contains references to the offer. Removing the promise seems to be a recent edit as an Internet Archive snapshot of the page from October 20 does mention the zero-day patch freebies.
A VMware spokesperson told us the free zero-day patch policy remains in place despite changes to the post.

“Broadcom’s policy to provide access to zero-day critical security patches to customers who, at their own risk, continue to run perpetual VMware vSphere 8 software without an active support agreement, remains in place,” the spokesperson wrote. “Those customers can get these patches by contacting Broadcom. This policy covers vSphere 8 patches only and is expected to remain in effect through the end of general support on October 11, 2027.” ®

18408ba5f27f7998: From Azrul Khalib

A medicine may be manufactured in Malaysia, packaged locally and supplied by a Malaysian company, yet still depend on a single factory overseas for a critical ingredient. If that factory shuts down or exports are disrupted, the local manufacturing line can also grind to a halt.

That is a vulnerability Malaysia cannot afford to overlook. We have invested billions of ringgit in hospitals, clinics, medical equipment and healthcare professionals. But the ability to deliver treatment ultimately depends on a less visible system: the supply chains that provide essential medicines.

Malaysia has a sizeable pharmaceutical industry, producing generic medicines, sterile preparations and other products while developing domestic human vaccine manufacturing capacity. But production is only one part of the chain. Manufacturers may still depend on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), chemical intermediates, excipients and specialised materials.

According to the Malaysian Investment Development Authority (Mida), pharmaceutical imports totalled RM11.30 billion in 2023, compared with RM2.92 billion in exports. An earlier Mida assessment found that approximately 39% of medicines on the National Essential Medicines List were imported. These figures underline Malaysia's reliance on international pharmaceutical trade, although they do not in themselves reveal how concentrated the country's upstream suppliers are.

That is the question policymakers need to ask. A manufacturer might have two suppliers in different countries, only to discover that both buy a key ingredient from the same upstream producer. What looks diversified on a procurement spreadsheet may be a single point of failure in practice.

Medicines are also harder to substitute than many other imported goods. Finding an alternative producer of an API is not the same as being able to use it immediately. Supplier audits, product validation, changes to regulatory documentation and approvals can take months. In a prolonged disruption, those delays matter.

Malaysia's ageing population and growing burden of non-communicable diseases make the continuity of treatment especially important. People living with diabetes, hypertension or cardiovascular disease need regular medicines. Hospitals depend on antibiotics, anaesthetics and critical-care products. Unlike a consumer purchase, treatment cannot always be postponed until prices fall or shipments resume.

More recent geopolitical tensions, tariffs and volatility in energy and shipping costs underscore why the next disruption may come from outside the pharmaceutical sector altogether. Inexpensive generic medicines, often produced and distributed on narrow margins, can be particularly exposed when costs rise or deliveries become uncertain.

China and India supply around 80% of bulk synthetic APIs, starting materials and complex generic powders to this country. India is Malaysia's primary foreign source for generic drugs, supplying roughly 30% of Malaysia's generic medicine and supplier base. The Covid-19 crisis and the geopolitical crises in 2026 have repeatedly raised vulnerabilities and risks to Malaysia should these countries decide impose export restrictions to protect their local supply of critical medicines.
The answer is not to manufacture everything domestically.

Instead, the government should start with the National Essential Medicines List and identify products whose interruption would cause the greatest harm. For those medicines, it should map not only where finished products are imported from, but where their APIs and other critical inputs actually originate. The exercise should distinguish genuine alternative manufacturers from distributors that ultimately rely on the same source.

That assessment should guide selective action. Some products may justify targeted incentives for domestic production, technology transfer or public-private manufacturing partnerships. Others may be better protected by qualifying alternative suppliers, arranging longer-term purchasing commitments or developing complementary manufacturing capacity with Asean partners.

Malaysia's New Industrial Master Plan 2030 already identifies pharmaceuticals, biologics and APIs as industrial development priorities. The next step is to connect those ambitions with actual healthcare vulnerabilities, rather than treating additional factory capacity as an end in itself.

Procurement policies also need to recognise that the lowest price is not necessarily the lowest cost. For strategically important medicines, buyers should consider the reliability of suppliers, geographic concentration, backup production capacity and whether alternative API sources have already been qualified.

Savings on a contract mean little if a subsequent shortage interrupts treatment. For vulnerable medicines, purchasing authorities should also consider advance ordering, contingency arrangements and whether contracts leave room for qualified backup suppliers. Such measures may carry a cost, but that cost should be assessed against the consequences of disrupted care.

Regional cooperation could strengthen this approach. Asean countries need not duplicate every expensive facility. Coordinated regulatory work, complementary production networks and emergency stock-sharing could create more options when an international supply chain fails.
Stockpiles remain important, but warehouses are not a substitute for supply-chain visibility.

Malaysia needs a more integrated monitoring system linking healthcare facilities, manufacturers, wholesalers and logistics providers so that emerging shortages can be detected early. The National Pharmaceutical Regulatory Agency's medicine-shortage and discontinuation reporting requirements are a useful foundation, but information is most valuable when it enables timely action.

Pharmaceutical supply resilience should be embedded in Malaysia's national health security planning, including its National Action Plan for Health Security 2025–2030. Success should be measured in fewer shortages, faster recovery, more qualified alternative sources and uninterrupted treatment, not simply in the number of pharmaceutical factories built.

Malaysia does not need to eliminate every foreign dependency. It needs to know which dependencies are critical, which are dangerously concentrated and how to reduce the risks before a disruption makes them visible to patients.
Azrul Khalib is the CEO of Galen Centre for Health and Social Policy, a health think tank.
