31d68f33a42508ee: Quick story, then some color on the price action1 this week:
I was at Bloomberg early yesterday for an 8:30 am podcast with Vlad Tenev, Robinhood’s founder and CEO (fun convo!).

Beforehand, a colleague asked me if I had any thoughts about the Anthropic IPO (specifically) and how markets have been behaving (generally). Mind you, this wasn’t on the air; it was just two guys bullshitting before the open.
I told him my thoughts, we talked a bit, then I went upstairs to record the pod.

After the pod, I sat in an empty cube, watching the 9:30 open, and seeing markets gap open hard while we all waited for Anthropic to price and start trading. I had my regular Thursday 11:30 radio hit coming up.
You can imagine my surprise when I heard my name on Bloomberg radio:

“…and Barry Ritholtz said before the open that markets have been ‘trading heavy’ and he is concerned that a big gap up might lead to an ‘intraday reversal;’ if we see markets close on their lows, well he says, Katie, bar the door.”

I recall saying most of that – except for the “Katy, bar the door” line; I am more of a “Look out below” kinda wordsmith. But really, I was just schmoozing with someone I know who has a trading background; it was much blunter and more technical than I would normally speak on air.
I feel compelled to add a bit more color on what I was thinking yesterday.
An intraday reversal occurs when markets gap up (down) and then give up those gains (make up those losses) to close at the market lows (highs).
The theory goes something like this: pre-market indications are driven by emotions, rumors, enthusiasm, fear, etc., and not the net balance or imbalance between supply and demand.

When we get large opening order imbalances, they sometimes drive markets to their day’s most extreme point, then cooler heads fade the open. By lunch, that opening gap gets filled, and the real battle between supply and demand begins, revealing who really controls price.

That’s the general gestalt of an intraday reversal, and it typically gives you some insight as to what’s gonna happen over the next few days or weeks. It’s fairly irrelevant to long-term investors, but matters a great deal to traders who live and die by their daily P&L. I was chatting with someone I think of as more of a trader than an investor, so I tailored my comments to them.
When I went on the air at 11:40, I explained my views: the markets had flipped back to green and were making up their losses, so I was glad not to contribute to a crowd panic.

Lots of enthusiasm for Anthropic (ANT) — perhaps too much? — and it seems to be sucking all of the oxygen and capital out of the room. SpaceX broke its IPO price; we will soon see if ANT does the same.
At the close, Nasdaq is down 5.3% for the day; semiconductors are down 11% for the day and 17% for the week…

33a61caea8aae9aa: Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples. Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview. Q: What were your goals for this project, and why would you opt to address AI models’ weaknesses over scaling to larger models?    A: This project has been going on for many years now, with roughly the same MIT-IBM team of speech and vision experts. We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data. Sometimes the models have seen certain phenomena, a latent representation of something that they have internally, but maybe due to subsequent fine-tuning or something, it disappears, so, developing techniques to try to make this capability re-emerge is a useful thing.  As you study these publicly available models, you can see weaknesses even in big ones, so I think it's important to try to address these limitations. If you had an unlimited budget, you could go out and create the annotations that you need, but it's also good to be able to try to get these models to learn more on their own. We’ve done that by creating novel benchmarks that we can evaluate against, then developing techniques that perform better on these benchmarks, and getting these models to learn on their own. Throughout our research collaboration — and this has very much been a strong collaboration between MIT and IBM — we have continued to release public benchmarks for people to use, and that's a lasting artifact. I think the overriding themes are multimodalities with language models, trying to address the shortcomings of these models, and trying to develop techniques that do not require a lot of annotated data to complete tasks better. Q: Can you walk us through how the project has evolved? A: When we first started this project, we were trying to build models that could learn correspondences automatically, not telling the machine anything more than, “This audio caption goes with this picture,” sort of like reading a picture book to a child who's learning language. We would just show it these matching examples, and we'd show it mismatching examples. They could learn that the sequence of sounds that says “lighthouse” corresponds to a picture of a lighthouse, without any text being involved. Moving beyond speech was to include general audio, and then we started looking at video instead of still images. We would train the model, showing it matching video sequences with the corresponding audio stream and then mismatching ones, and make it reconstruct them. We would also mask some of the images or the audio, and have the model reconstruct it. The model would learn strong relationships; then, far beyond speech, it would learn what parrots sound like, or electric guitars versus acoustic guitars, for example. Then, when these large language models started coming out — and this was in the early days, before it had been done by the big companies — we started to learn correspondences between audio and language. Since that time, these large multimodal models have become available, and we've started looking at what some of the limitations of these models are, and are trying to improve upon them with these more or less supervised techniques. Q: What would you say are some recent highlights of your work? A: Our IPLoc research was looking at the fact that these state-of-the-art models, like GPT-40, can't localize specific objects, given just a few-shot examples. We came up with this technique where we would train it with a pseudonym substitution. There's an example there where we replaced “airplane” with “Elizabeth.” It forces the model to not fall back on things that it had previously learned about and pay more attention to the visual context. Then, we had an audio-based paper, OmniR1, that was looking at audio-large language models, so these are models that can listen to something and talk about them. One of the disturbing things we found is some of these benchmarks are multiple-choice answers. A lot of times, these models aren't really listening to the sound, but they're almost gaming the question by looking at the answer. What animal is roaring in this audio — like a chipmunk, a lion, an alligator, and a chickadee, or something? It's not even really paying attention to the audio, [but] just going, “Oh, lion.” Part of the reason people do that is that it’s simple to evaluate, whereas if you asked for a text response, you’d somehow have to grade whether it’s accurate. Do you get humans to evaluate it, which can be expensive and time-consuming, or do you use some other language model to be the judge that can have its own set of issues as well? One way to address that is to evaluate these models on a variety of different kinds of benchmarks. We realized you could feed random noise, and they were still doing quite well, which shows that they're just paying attention to the question. So, we tried to develop some methods to have it pay more attention to the audio and minimize this behavior. Q: Given resource constraints, what is your approach to adapting these large foundation models, and what blend of AI and algorithmic methods do you use that don't require extensive annotated data? A: These days, we can't create one of these very large foundation models ourselves. We don't have the resources to do that, so we're tending to use these available models and trying to adapt them, train them in a weakly supervised way, methods that don't require as much data, like our work on test-time reinforcement learning. Our project was not monolithic, in the sense that we're not all working on one thing. It's more like a thousand flowers bloom, so there's no one particular way that we're approaching things. Q: In the near future, how do you see multimodal research evolving in your MIT-IBM research team? A: Over the years, we probably produced two dozen or so significant collaborative papers, and during this work, it was amazing to me that the machines could learn these correspondences without being told anything. No one had ever shown that machines could do it before we did that. Some of our early work combining audio with large language models was fun, too: seeing the model talk about what it heard and then having a conversation with it. Now, we are starting to take this for granted, but at the time, it was fun to see. Moving forward, for the coming year, with our MIT-IBM collaboration, we're going to switch gears a little bit and focus more on what's known as full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. These are models that are listening while they’re talking, so it’s more like how humans operate, and this is quite different from what we’ve been doing up until now, which is joint audio-visual work, which we will also continue.  Now, we’ll be focusing on the speech side of things. These full-duplex models have suddenly become an interesting thing to look at, because they would move you away from the rigid turn-taking approach that is used right now when you're talking to some of these models. Ultimately, I think they will be more natural to interact with.  These full-duplex models are just starting to emerge, and some of the ones that are publicly available aren't as good as the big, large language models. They can handle some of these low-level communication skills, but they're still missing some things, like the concept of time, or knowledge depth. So, we're working on trying to address some of these issues. This research has been conducted in coordination with the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab teams of Rogerio Feris, Brian Kingsbury, and Samuel Thomas of IBM Research, and Hilde Kuehne of the University of Tuebingen, who is an MIT-IBM affiliated researcher.
6e086317ffb3ab4e: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. 9a45945e8feac5d2: In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.

In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”

Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.

480a8b723958aa8d: Modeling of complex, chaotic processes such as weather and climate patterns and turbulent flows in aviation or in ocean currents has advanced enormously in recent years. However, such models are still prone to drift into physically impossible predictions over time. Now, researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models that can ensure that such models never exceed realistic bounds, based on what is actually possible in the real world. This new approach, using information that is now being made freely available by the team, could significantly improve the usefulness and reliability of such models, which besides climate and weather are also used in a wide range of industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology. The new findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis.  “Lack of guarantees for a bounded response has always been a major obstacle on formulating data-driven models for complex nonlinear systems,” says Sapsis, a professor of mechanical engineering and LIDS affiliate. The approach the team has developed, he says, “paves the way for applying the most advanced machine-learning architectures for prediction and control in a plethora of real-world problems, even those characterized by intrinsic instabilities.” Developing reliable models for complex dynamical systems is important across many domains. In fluid dynamics, turbulent flows can disrupt air travel, reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, and affect fuel economy of vehicles. Similarly, in weather forecasting, the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics makes accurate long-term predictions difficult.  “Tiny differences in the starting conditions can lead to dramatically different outcomes in a chaotic system,” Azizan says. “That makes predicting its behavior far into the future extremely difficult.” And yet, there are always physical constraints on the kinds of changes that are possible in the real world. “Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.” But how to introduce those boundaries into the models has been a thorny problem, says Azizan, the Hayes Associate Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, and a principal investigator in LIDS. “A model can match the data over a short period and still fail when you let it run for a long time,” he says. “Small errors can accumulate until the simulation produces values that grow without limit,” producing predictions that could never actually occur in real systems. “It’s a fundamental problem with many of the existing machine learning models,” he says. “It’s a question that comes up frequently in different domains: how can we embed physical constraints into these models in a way that preserves their flexibility, but ensures physically meaningful outputs?” “We want to preserve the chaos without the artificial runaway behavior that the real system does not have,” he says. “Our approach gives the model room to learn complex dynamics while guaranteeing that its trajectories stay bounded.” This is the first work that establishes such formal guarantees for machine learning models of chaos. Previous attempts to prevent unrealistic results from such models have often been based on “imposing penalties or incentives during training,” says Tang, a doctoral student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and LIDS, using functions that are often designed based on privileged information about the system. But as these only apply during the training process for the model, “there’s no guarantee that the model will satisfy the underlying constraints intended by such incentives at test time” once it is dealing with new inputs when it is actually used. “The model could still produce unbounded predictions,” he says. To illustrate why simply imposing arbitrary limits would not be a satisfactory solution to the prediction stability issue, Tang explains, “you can cap the predictions, for example, by setting an arbitrary limit on physical quantities, such as 100 degrees for temperature. That’s one possible way to keep predictions bounded, but it could restrict the model from representing complex and nontrivial features that should be learned directly from the data.” He says that “what sets our approach apart is that we formulate energy-based constraints. We let the model learn an energy-like function,” based on real-world chaotic systems, where energy dissipation helps keep trajectories bounded despite their complex behaviors. “Specifically, the model learns an energy-like function, along with a boundary where its chaotic behavior should be confined to. We then add a projection layer, a component that adjusts how the model predicts the system will evolve, to enforce energy dissipation as a hard constraint. Outside this boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, so the simulated system is drawn toward the bounded region. That way, we can establish theoretical guarantees that the model prediction remains bounded over arbitrarily long forecast windows.” The team tested their approach on a variety of different well-known physical systems, ranging from simple textbook cases to highly complex multidimensional systems, and found that their approach closely matched the true outcomes, while conventional approaches soon deviated into impossible predictions. Azizan adds that “the fundamental difference between our approach and the existing approaches is what we call hard constraining versus soft constraining.” While many of the current approaches “try to incentivize the model to satisfy the constraints, they’re not treated as hard constraints. Our approach is based on the concept of hard-constrained neural networks,” so that what comes out “is always physically consistent, even if it’s a completely new case the model hasn’t seen.” “AI models shine in scenarios where there’s a large amount of data available,” Azizan says, for example with images or with text, both of which are abundantly available on the internet. However, he says, “for a lot of physical systems, data is not as abundant.” For such cases where the data is limited, he says, “these physics-constrained approaches can help a lot, because the physics of the problem is another source of information.” The new approach is broadly useful for any chaotic systems. “This is readily applicable to a wide range of neural network architectures,” Tang says. They plan to continue testing it on ever-larger systems. “We’re trying to see how well this would work on data-driven models of realistic weather systems.” “The projection layer is modular: it is model-agnostic and can work with different neural network architectures,” Azizan says. “We hope other researchers and practitioners will build on it and test it on larger and even more complex problems.” The paper, along with open-source code, is now accessible online at PNAS. A follow-up work this year by members of the team was presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference. The paper won the conference’s Best Paper Award. “Trustworthy and reliable AI needs more than just evidence that a model usually works,” Azizan says. “For high-stakes applications, you need guarantees about the properties that must always hold. In this work, we established one such guarantee: boundedness. Our broader goal is to make principles part of how AI models are built, not just how they are tested.”
c4fcf3d7ab6e8c9f: A 'Saturday Night Live' parody commercial delivered a sobering message to America about a widespread problem. Alican Lazutti/iStock via Getty Images Plus“Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people. The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains. I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story. A growing trend One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes. My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults. The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion. The “Sister” sketch on “Saturday Night Live” has launched a national conversation about caregiving. Warning: ‘Sister’ may break down Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price. Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people. That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Family caregivers pay a price Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour, totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460. But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones. Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one. AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. ‘Sister’ lampoons gender roles in caring for aging family members. NBC A ‘daughterhood penalty’ Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “daughterhood penalty,” or tax. Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability. Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives. But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing. Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores. Patricia Smith is affiliated with the Ottawa County, MI Democratic Party.
00aa8aae69bf041d: The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:

The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

CTIA said the pilot test shows "that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications."
f193d99c3cb1adeb: In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

"Public communication is essential to public trust," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. "Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."
583b7a1c74131e15: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.

The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared—and widely misinterpreted, owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled.

The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work.

It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development.

And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor of two. That report sparked fears that the company (which just had a blockbuster IPO) could soon achieve full recursive self-improvement, a regime in which AI systems autonomously design their own successors with no human involvement.

METR researchers have worked to make sure their new suite of tasks includes some of the fuzzier, judgment-laden ones that could be most relevant to AI research and development. In one task, they ask models to design new AI evaluations that METR could use in its research and then have human METR employees score the results. Even though the most advanced models are now better than almost every human at software engineering, here they fall short: Not one of the AI-designed evaluations was good enough for METR employees to consider it useful for their research.

In another task, models have to score philosophical arguments. This task is intended to capture the extent to which models can exercise good judgment—though METR writes in the report that employees disagree about how relevant the task is for automation of AI R&D. On this task, too, models fell short of human performance.

Though it’s difficult to score these new tasks—and even harder to determine what the scores mean—experts I spoke with appreciate that METR is incorporating new types of evaluations into its work. “We’re at the point where AI evaluations need to get more creative,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist and incoming professor at UC Berkeley. “Trying to push the envelope of the space of evaluations is a welcome change.”

Kapoor says he wasn’t surprised to see that models fall short of performance on more open-ended tasks, such as designing an AI evaluation—in a preprint from August, he and his collaborators reported that AI models are not yet able to reproduce human computer science research on their own. And in a Wednesday blog post, OpenAI reported that its models don’t do as well on the real-world tasks its employees assign them as they do on the easier, more verifiable tasks in METR’s original suite.

Still, people disagree about how to interpret current performance differences on easily verifiable and hard-to-verify tasks, Kapoor says. Though he thinks that research taste—the ability to choose promising questions, hypotheses, and experiments—will prove a major bottleneck in automating AI R&D, others contend that models trained on easy-to-verify tasks will eventually be able to successfully complete open-ended tasks as well. And progress on verifiable tasks doesn’t seem to be slowing down.

Even if the models do lag behind human performance on open-ended tasks right now, the new report suggests that they might be getting better. Some of the newest models, such as Opus 5.5, tend to achieve what METR calls “borderline above the bar” performance on the evaluation design tasks—not yet usable for METR’s research, but promising. Just a year ago, every model was scoring in the “clearly below the bar” category.

But because these open-ended and judgment-heavy tasks are so tough to design and score, METR includes few of them in its report, and that makes it difficult to predict whether and how models might continue to progress in these areas. “The improvement we observe, I think that does tell us something for the current moment,” says Najoung Kim, a linguist and computer scientist at Boston University. “I’m not sure just yet how to think about how it would extrapolate.”

Matt Putz, a member of the technical staff at METR, says that predicting progress on these kinds of tasks is likely to remain difficult. “By their nature, hard-to-verify or judgment-laden tasks are much harder to study, and especially to quantify,” he said in an email. “Ultimately, I don’t think we’ll be able to establish trends as clean and robust as for the easy-to-specify [tasks].”

In general, METR is clearly butting up against the practical difficulties of testing AI performance on difficult and underspecified tasks—precisely the ones most relevant to automating AI R&D. METR’s time horizon plots score task difficulty by evaluating how long it would take a human to complete the task, and for the original plot they measured this quantity by actually having people try each task.

In the new report, however, the completion times are mostly estimates, because paying people for tasks that might take hundreds of hours, or that only a few experts are qualified to complete, is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. Other tasks have more specific shortcomings—for example, for the philosophical argument task, just one person rated most of the arguments, and agents are judged by how well they agree with that particular individual. It’s possible that the scores would change if more experts were surveyed—but that, too, is time-consuming.

It’s still early days for evaluating models on tasks that are hard to validate or require judgment. And while the experts I spoke with see the inclusion of these tasks in METR’s newest time horizon plot as a clear step in the right direction, they agree that we are still far from achieving any definitive answers about whether, and how quickly, automated AI R&D might be coming. “This move toward open-ended tasks is promising,” Kapoor says. But, he adds, “there is just such a lot more to be done to actually get a fuller understanding.”
59d932d229ff420e: Activists want to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment and punish those responsible for defiling it
Originally published on Global Voices

An aerial view of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, the largest marine oil spill in history. Under the proposed ICC amendment, oil company executives could be held accountable in such cases. Image via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 2.0.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In September 2024, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Samoa filed an amendment request at the International Criminal Court (ICC) to get “ecocide” recognized as a crime under international law. The ICC currently recognizes four criminal categories: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression.

Over two years later, the amendment is still formally pending; but that does not mean environmental activists are waiting around — in fact, many are working both in the public eye and behind the scenes to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment, combat the climate crisis, and punish those responsible for defiling the planet.

According to an independent expert panel convened by the Stop Ecocide Foundation, ecocide is legally defined as “unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and either widespread or long-term damage to the environment being caused by those acts.”
For the countries that backed the proposal, the climate crisis is not an abstract threat; it is a real and present danger with active consequences for their people.

In 2021, Simon Kofe, Tuvalu’s Minister for Justice, Communication and Foreign Affairs, gave a presentation at the international COP26 conference on climate change while standing in knee-deep water to demonstrate how rising sea levels threaten low-lying island nations. Tuvaluan officials are also exploring ways to become the first “digital nation” as a backup plan in case rising sea levels submerge all livable land in the archipelago. In Fiji alone, six villages have already been relocated because of climate change, with others in progress and dozens more under assessment. As Vanuatu’s Special Envoy for Climate Change and Environment, Ralph Regenvanu, says, climate damage is “devastating our island economy, submerging our territory, and threatening livelihoods.”

Shortly after the amendment was submitted, it was also backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is experiencing increasingly deadly flooding as well as air quality issues related to exploitative mining operations.
Tuvulu’s Foreign Minister delivers an address to COP26, while standing in knee-deep water to illustrate how rising sea levels threaten Pacific nations. Image from Simon Kofe’s Facebook. Fair use.

It is not a coincidence that those who are pushing hardest for these legal mechanisms are those most affected by the climate crisis. These nations did little to cause the crisis, while major superpowers like the U.S., China, and Europe, as well as the corporations that bolster them, have made billions by exploiting and polluting the environment unchecked.

Meanwhile, those who suffer from the consequences of our eroding climate have limited legal recourse against the corporations and states most responsible. This juxtaposition is where the argument to make ecocide an international crime comes in.
Vanuatu was the first state to call for ecocide to be added to the ICC in 2019. In announcing the proposal, Regenvanu said:

“We are taking bold and necessary action to address these challenges and encourage other vulnerable states to take note of our newly tabled proposal to bring ecocide to the ICC. Legal recognition of severe and widespread environmental harm holds significant potential to ensure justice and, crucially, to deter further destruction.”
A protest poster against ecocide shaming oil giants at a climate protest in Maryland in 2017. Photo from Wikimedia Commons. CC BY-SA 2.0.
Why reform the ICC?

The International Criminal Court was formally established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for grave international crimes (not to be confused with the International Court of Justice, which settles legal disputes between countries).

Environmental crimes are particularly tricky, as traditional legal accountability measures tend to rely on specific individuals or property that have been harmed in order to pursue legal action. In cases where polluters are contributing to a broader destructive pattern, the legal standing becomes murky. This theory has been tested numerous times as individuals have sought to sue fossil fuel companies in civil court for their destructive practices and malfeasance, with most cases largely unsuccessful.

Supporters say that if the proposed amendment were successful, it would give ICC prosecutors the power to hold individuals, such as the executives of large polluting companies or heads of state, responsible in cases like massive oil spills or the deforestation of essential rainforests.
As an editorial in The Global Witness notes:

While there have been a series of recent valiant attempts to sue fossil fuel corporations in civil court for covering up evidence that their activities were causing global warming, the defendants have largely been able to get away scot-free. … Criminalizing ecocide would fill this legal gap, and allow individuals (and companies in some jurisdictions) to be prosecuted for engaging in acts with knowledge that they are substantially likely to damage the environment, without the need to show harm to any individual person.

To add a crime to the Rome Statute, a proposal must win a two-thirds majority vote within the court’s Assembly of States Parties. Even then, an amendment to the statute’s crimes provisions would bind only the states that accept it, and the court could not prosecute nationals or territory of states that do not.

The Rome Statute has 123 signatory parties — a number that does not include China, India, or the U.S., the world’s three largest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. The U.S., in particular, under current President Donald Trump’s administration, has backed away from climate commitments in recent years, including withdrawing from the UN’s 2015 Paris Climate Agreement. It has also become increasingly hostile toward the court itself, as the Trump administration imposed sanctions on individual ICC prosecutors and judges beginning in early 2025. Then, in a September 2026 address to the UN General Assembly, Trump urged all member states to withdraw from the treaty altogether, and, weeks later, in October 2026, he imposed sweeping sanctions on the court itself.

With the biggest emitters outside the court, and Washington working to undermine it, advocates are looking beyond The Hague and ICC reform. As legal watchdogs argue, the end goal is not merely to get the ICC to recognize ecocide — though that would be an excellent first step — rather, if the ICC were to establish a framework for prosecuting international environmental crimes, through an amendment or merely by adapting its existing policies, this could push ratifying states to update their domestic penal codes and adopt policies to protect and preserve their own ecosystems, and also prosecute those who violate them.
Existing provisions within the Rome Statute
The International Criminal Court (ICC) at The Hague. Photo via Wikimedia Commons. CC BY 2.0.
Even though the proposal has thus far not been adopted by the ICC, the court has not stood still.

In December 2025, ICC prosecutors published a policy paper on prosecuting environmental damage through the pre-existing mechanisms already laid out in the Rome Statute — the international treaty which established the ICC.

The Rome Statute mentions the environment exactly one time. Article 8(2)(b)(iv) makes it a war crime to launch an attack knowing it will cause “widespread, long-term and severe” damage to the environment. Traditionally, this article has applied only during armed conflict, and previous attempts to prosecute environmental destruction at the court have been unsuccessful.
Vanuatu’s ambassador to the UN, Odo Tevi, has argued that the reckless destruction of nature “can and does take place at any time, not just during conflict.”

The December 2025 policy, launched at the Assembly of States Parties, was co-hosted by Costa Rica, France, Germany, Panama, and the Marshall Islands. It explains how environmental destruction can be investigated and prosecuted within the four existing crime categories, for example, when pollution or the seizure of natural resources is used to commit a crime against humanity.

Analysts at the Conflict and Environment Observatory note that this policy paper does not address the ecocide proposal and that ambiguity in the war crime standard remains. Others point to limited resources at the prosecutor’s office.

In September 2026, ICC representatives said they had “moved into the implementation stage” to establish clearer parameters for prosecuting environmental crimes under the Rome Statute. In its statement, the office said it had received numerous communications about alleged crimes with an environmental dimension and was building a network of environmental law enforcement authorities, relevant organizations, expert groups, and civil society organizations to investigate.

But some jurisdictions are not waiting. As one recent study notes, “the substance of ecocide criminalization has advanced everywhere except through the amendment: an EU directive whose gravest offense is officially ‘comparable to “ecocide,”’ a Council of Europe convention, national codes in Belgium, France and Ukraine, and a completed OTP [ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor] policy that prosecutes environmental damage through the existing four crimes.”

Counts vary depending on how many states currently employ domestic laws against ecocide. Stop Ecocide International says twelve countries, including Belgium, France, and Ukraine, have adopted ecocide or equivalent offenses into domestic law. Mauritius became the most recent in April 2026, and legislation is progressing in countries including Brazil, Peru, Argentina, Mexico, Italy, and the Netherlands.

As noted in the aforementioned study, the EU’s revised Environmental Crime Directive also covers conduct “comparable to ecocide,” and member states had to transpose it by May 2026. Additionally, legal and environmental experts from 14 Latin American countries published a model ecocide law on October 1, 2026, in an effort to jumpstart future ecocide laws in the region.
What comes next

The next stage is procedural rather than dramatic: Whether states give the proposal a formal path forward at the Assembly of States Parties’ 25th session in The Hague, from November 30 to December 7, 2026. A vote would signal whether the Rome Statute can grow beyond the atrocities it was written for. A stall would leave the prosecutor’s policy and national laws as the main tools available.
The decision comes at a crucial time for the ICC, as some international stakeholders begin to question the legitimacy, power, and effectiveness of international ruling bodies.

For the nations that started this, the stakes are not abstract. They are asking the world to build infrastructure to prosecute and prevent harm that is already happening to them. 9be98e73c6c88adf: It’s been a tumultuous year for math. Big open questions that have occupied mathematicians for decades are now being solved in a matter of hours by artificial intelligence agents that companies deploy by the thousands to work on a single problem in tireless lockstep.  AI’s relentless rise is raising existential questions for the field: How will the tools affect humans’ understanding of mathematical concepts? In the face of AI’s brute-force productivity, will mathematicians still have jobs? And what will all this mean for mathematics as an intellectual pursuit?  At MIT, mathematicians grappled with these and other questions at a panel discussion on Monday titled “AI and Society: The Future of Math.” Leading mathematicians from MIT, Harvard University, Northwestern University, and New York University — each experts in their respective fields — sat down for a conversation that touched on the quality of AI math, how AI is challenging long-established research norms, and the evolving opportunities for mathematicians, whether they embrace the machines or remain “AI vegans.” The wide-ranging discussion, which took place in a packed lecture hall in MIT’s Building 3, was moderated by science writer Kevin Hartnett, author of “The Proof in the Code,” and featured Jacopo Borga, the Cecil and Ida Green Career Development Assistant Professor of Mathematics at MIT; Michael Hopkins, the George Putnam Professor of Pure and Applied Mathematics at Harvard University; Bryna Kra, the Sarah Rebecca Roland Professor of Mathematics at Northwestern University; and Tristan Buckmaster, professor of mathematics at New York University's Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences. As the panelists shared their various and at times conflicting perspectives on AI’s impact, one thing was clear: “Math has changed more in the last two months than in the last 100 years,” said Kra, who cautioned that AI’s power will change what it is to be a mathematician and what it will take to advance human knowledge in meaningful ways. “It’s like the first sentence in ‘A Tale of Two Cities’: ‘It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.’ It’s a really exciting moment … and also scary.” AI’s sprint Artificial intelligence has made steady strides over the last decade thanks in large part to mathematicians themselves, who out of curiosity have been honing AI models to solve problems with known solutions. These early exercises proved successful, most notably in 2025. That summer, at the International Mathematical Olympiad, Google DeepMind’s AI models achieved gold-medal status by quickly finding solutions to most of the problems that were posed to the world’s best high school mathematicians.  Around that same time, other mathematicians found that some AI systems could solve problems with known solutions, but in ways that were slightly improved compared to the solutions that human mathematicians had derived.  In 2026, AI’s power took a quantum leap. In several instances, scientists found that models could solve open-ended research questions — mathematical problems that had no known answer. Then, in September, OpenAI made a field-shaking announcement: The company focused thousands of its AI agents on a singular challenge, and after 88 hours, the agents produced a proof related to the Navier-Stokes equation — a Millienum Prize Problem that is one of seven unsolvable mathematical Holy Grails.  OpenAI’s sudden interest in the Navier-Stokes challenge coincided with work by Tristan Buckmaster, one of the panelists. After a year of progress, he and his collaborator, at rival AI behemoth Anthropic, were on the cusp of solving the problem when OpenAI made its announcement. OpenAI’s sprint to be first to the proof opened up a huge debate, about whether proper credit was given, whether the mathematicians’ data was leaked, how the AI agents arrived at their solution, whether that solution makes any meaningful sense, and above all, how AI will change mathematical research.  A month later, the company doubled down, releasing 722 manuscripts, organized into categories that ran the gamut of mathematical topics. The manuscripts claimed to have used AI entirely to solve many of math’s major, unsolved problems — an achievement that has widely been coined the “mathocalypse.”  But many mathematicians insist that it isn’t just about whether a problem can be solved, but also, how. And, they say, when they’ve looked into the details of AI proofs, it’s not clear how the agents arrived at their conclusions.  “The papers themselves are nonsense,” Hopkins said during Monday’s discussion, noting that AI-generated proofs contain “strange ideas.” He continued: “There still is a sense of AI math versus human math.” “For math to be important, it has to have human understanding,” Buckmaster added.  New norms For mathematicians like Kra, this moment in math’s history presents an opportunity to let go of certain long-held norms of mathematical research, such as competition among research groups and the prestige of being the first to prove an idea, also known as priority. “It shouldn’t matter that you’re first,” Kra said. “Speed should not be a priority. It’s not about the proof production anymore. We need to find other ways to assess understanding.” However, “We can throw away priority, but people are going to want to be pioneers,” Hopkins countered, noting the challenge that mathematicians will now face in making in-roads where AI has already clear-cut.  Kra, however, struck a hopeful counterpoint:  “You can be a pioneer in different ways, for instance in communicating [how a proof came to be],” said Kra, who helped this year to draft the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics — a statement signed by mathematicians around the world that calls for action to address the risks that AI poses to mathematical research. “Communication of math is even more important now.”  Indeed, the panelists have already seen a subtle shift in what is expected of a mathematician, at all levels, from undergraduate students to early and established career mathematicians.  “The interview is becoming more important,” said Kra, noting that it’s no longer enough to accept, hire, or promote a mathematician based on ideas they have written or published — they have to also show that they understand and can explain those ideas to another person.  Human math AI is also making mathematicians question the role of academic journals, which have long been the benchmark for evaluating and validating mathematical advances. “Ninety percent of how we’ve judged [mathematicians] are through journals,” says Jacopo Borga, who is an early-career mathematician at MIT. “I’m not sure that’s how we should do this anymore. We should come up with a new metric and let it evolve.” Kra, who is a managing editor of a specialty journal, is seeing a huge increase in the number of papers submitted, primarily reporting results that were generated or assisted by AI. To deal with the deluge, that particular journal has had to hire an additional managing editor.  Where journal editors have traditionally prioritized publishing new proofs that push the field forward, Kra sees that, in response to AI “slop,” some publications are putting more value on exposition — the section of a paper that explains the reasoning behind a conjecture or proof. For now, humans have the advantage over AI in communicating mathematical ideas. “There’s a real art to exposition, if you can explain something in a clear and elegant way,” Hopkins echoed.  Kra noted that there are experimental journals coming online now, that are designed to highlight uniquely human contributions to mathematics. For instance, there are journals that publish expositions, such as papers that explain an old result in a new way that modern mathematicians can understand. “There is a lot of opportunity to curate and translate knowledge,” said Hopkins, who shared that one of his students has been working to prove a theorem from the 1970s. The original language and construction from that decades-old theorem, he said, was just as foreign as some of AI’s proofs today.  In noting novel approaches journals are taking in response to AI, Kra also mentioned Mathematical Discourse, a new peer-reviewed “video journal” that will feature videos of people giving talks about mathematical research. The journal’s preliminary site states that “giving a mathematical talk captures the human side of mathematics in a unique way, and supporting these human aspects of our discipline will be ever more important in the coming years.” “A new kind of mathematician” The rise of AI may be hitting especially hard for students, who are still learning the fundamentals in the presence of so many AI shortcuts.  “Mathematics is probably the slowest science you can do,” said Borga, to appreciative laughs from the audience. “Students today are bombarded by [conflicting messages of] what they should do, and are overwhelmed. We need to give them space to learn.” How they should learn could be a matter of personal belief.  “There is a big faction of my group who are ‘AI vegans’ [people who do not use AI], while others are using it,” said Hopkins, who is finding ways to support both groups. He also highlighted one particular student, who seemed to be a sort of “horse whisperer of AI.” This student has good mathematical instincts, Hopkins said, but struggles with execution. They are motivated by curiosity, rather than being first to a solution, and have a way of prompting AI to produce interesting insights.  “This may be a new kind of mathematician,” Hopkins said.  As AI forces the field of mathematics to adapt and change its centuries-long ways of pursuing knowledge, Borga and others see the moment as a new beginning, rather than math’s end. “The castle is collapsing,” Borga says. “There’s open ground to explore.” “AI is going to affect everyone (beyond mathematicians),” said Buckmaster, who urged students to stay the course “rather than escape or jump ship to another field. … Think of new ways to be creative and communicate your ideas,” he said. “Just do what you love.” The panel discussion, co-sponsored by the Department of Mathematics, is the first of a planned series hosted by MITHIC and SERC exploring how AI is reshaping our personal and professional lives.

165fadc595acce83: Andy Burnham has attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels with major agreements reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. Ultimately though, the prime minister will have understood that this was merely the start of new political negotiations. Back home in the UK, he has started a “national conversation” on the future of UK-EU relations that gained momentum rapidly. Burnham held talks with European Council president Antonio Costa and president of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. Both Burnham and Costa come from sister social democratic parties and both are former mayors – Burnham of Greater Manchester and Costa of Lisbon. This could make for smoother meetings in future than in the months and years after the 2016 Brexit referendum. In the run up to the talks, the prime minister had repeatedly claimed that the Conservatives failed to get a good deal from the EU. As part of former prime minister Keir Starmer’s “reset” of relations with Europe, then-business secretary, Peter Kyle, and European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera signed a deal committing the UK and the EU to closer cooperation on trade. Like Costa and Burnham, Ribera is also from a European social democratic party (the Spanish Socialist Workers Party, or PSOE). Senior figures in Labour have long admired the electoral success of social democrats in both Spain and Portugal. When it comes to claims of the UK having had a bad deal, there is one explanation that is under-discussed. It has its roots in the internal party politics of the centre-right in Europe. Ahead of the 2009 European Parliament elections, the then-Conservative leader David Cameron decided to leave the European People’s Party (a bloc of centre-right pro-European parties). Cameron went on to set up a new right-of-centre eurosceptic faction with parties from Poland and the Czech Republic. But he underestimated how hurt highly influential EU figures like German chancellor Angela Merkel were by the move. So when it came to negotiating a better deal with the EU ahead of the 2016 referendum, Merkel and other figures had not forgotten Cameron’s betrayal. As such, they felt disinclined to meet him half way. Burnham is walking a fine line Youth mobility, migration, food exports and emissions are all important issues. But the broader discussion is increasingly about the politics around Brexit rather than the rights and wrongs of Brexit itself. The UK is not going to rejoin the EU in the near future. Burnham even said when standing in the Makerfield byelection that first and foremost he wants to sort the consequences of Brexit rather than necessarily the outcome. Now Burnham is increasingly focused on the claim that Brexit hasn’t worked for British voters – without saying it was completely wrong. He may understand that aiming to reverse Brexit in a binary way could simply open up new problems. It could even finish his premiership in the same way that it ended the tenures of multiple prime ministers before him. In contrast, however, Burnham understands that he has the political capital to discuss the downsides of Brexit. For now, at least, he can do this in a way that is unlikely to result in much political damage to his government. While not completely without risk, he has calculated that the benefits of discussing Brexit outweigh any costs. These costs could include the fragile “red wall” of Labour seats in northern England and the Midlands. The party knows all too well that this could flip to Reform UK the next time the country goes to the polls. But those voters who have already moved to Reform are something of a sunk cost for Labour. For now, it seems Burnham sees more advantages in drawing voters away from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens than he sees disadvantages in alienating supporters of Reform. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch appears to be sensitive to the fact that many people disapprove of how the Tories handled Brexit – whether they voted Remain or Leave. At the height of the Brexit chaos, however, Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester and so can revisit the issue in a fresh way, untainted by the Westminister turbulence of that time. His predecessor Starmer was frequently seen as being paralysed by caution. Burnham appears to know how to talk about difficult issues lightly and fluently – his own parliamentary seat overwhelmingly voted Leave in 2016. He may or may not truly want to see the UK rejoin the EU at some point – he has sometimes sent out mixed signals on the issue. But he certainly has the firm aim of removing the toxicity from the issue and having a “national conversation”. To do this, the prime minister will have to consider how Westminster relates to Brussels as well as how it relates to constituencies like his own in Makerfield. 449ce2f82209367a: A recent 'SNL' sketch called 'Sister' lampoons gender roles in caring for aging parents. NBCA “Saturday Night Live” sketch that introduced a fictional elder care service simply called “Sister” has gone viral. The premise was simple: Why pay for professional care for an aging parent when a daughter can do it for free? The clip, which first aired on Nov. 15, 2026, struck a nerve because this kind of arrangement is familiar and burdensome for millions of American families. According to a 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving, 63 million Americans provide ongoing care to a family member or friend, an increase of nearly 50% over the past decade. About 61% of these caregivers are women. As researchers who study aging, long-term care and financial security, we’ve found that those who become caregivers initially have better health and financial status than noncaregivers. But they then experience relatively worse health and financial decline over time compared with their noncaregiving counterparts. While societal gender expectations help explain why daughters often assume the bulk of caregiving responsibilities, government policies have also determined how much care families must provide. “Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch immediately went viral. Medicare doesn’t cover long-term care One of the most consequential features of America’s long-term care system is that Medicare, the federal health insurance program covering most adults 65 and older, generally does not pay for ongoing care and assistance with everyday activities. Medicare covers hospitalizations, physician visits and certain home health services. However, those who need help with daily tasks such as bathing, dressing, preparing meals or getting to the bathroom generally cannot rely on Medicare to pay for that assistance. Under Medicare’s home health benefit, limited personal care may be covered only when a patient also qualifies for skilled nursing or therapy services following surgery or a medical emergency and meets Medicare’s homebound requirements. This distinction has enormous consequences. Someone over 65 may have comprehensive coverage for medical treatment but little help with the daily tasks necessary to remain safely at home. And this care is expensive: The national median cost of a home health aide was approximately US$6,688 per month, while residing in an assisted living facility averaged $6,141 per month in 2025. For many older Americans, paying for the care they need is simply out of reach. A 2025 Harvard study found that 76% of households age 75 and older could not afford daily assistance from a home health aide after covering housing and basic living expenses. When paid care is unaffordable, those responsibilities frequently fall to relatives or, more rarely, close friends. Medicaid can help, but access is limited Medicaid, the public health insurance program for people who are low-income or have disabilities, is the country’s primary long-term care payer. Unlike Medicare, Medicaid can pay for personal assistance at home, including help with bathing, dressing and other daily activities. The program covered nearly two-thirds of U.S. home care spending in 2023. The divide between these programs dates back to 1965, when Medicare was created to cover medical care for older adults, while Medicaid was designed to provide health coverage for people with low incomes. Over time, Medicaid became the country’s main payer for long-term care as the need for these costly services grew. However, Medicaid eligibility generally requires meeting financial and other criteria that vary by state. Many older adults must exhaust most of their savings before qualifying for assistance. Even being eligible for the program doesn’t guarantee that all needed services will be readily available. States have considerable discretion over the home-based services they provide, and many eligible people spend more than a year on waitlists to get services. Who provides care in the meantime? As the sketch suggests, daughters are more likely to care for their aging parents. Visual Vic/Moment via Getty Images There’s a shortage of paid caregivers Having coverage, whether through Medicaid or the dwindling options available through private insurers to pay for long-term care, is only part of the challenge. Finding reliable help can be a struggle. The nation’s direct care workforce, which includes home health aides and personal care assistants, faces persistent recruitment and retention challenges. These shortages may get worse as immigration enforcement and deportations reduce the workforce – one-third of these workers are foreign-born. The median hourly wage for direct care work was $17.99 in 2025, only $2-$3 per hour more than what fast-food workers earned. Caregiving often has financial consequences When paid assistance is unavailable, insufficient or unaffordable, daughters and other relatives often fill the gaps by providing additional hours of care. Family caregivers may have to work fewer hours or quit their jobs. These decisions not only reduce their income right away, but also whittle down their retirement savings and can depress the Social Security benefits they get in the future. The federal Family and Medical Leave Act provides eligible workers with up to 12 weeks of job-protected leave to care for certain family members, but the leave is unpaid. And caring for an older parent with chronic health conditions may continue for years after that leave runs out. Because women are more likely to provide family care, they also face disproportionate exposure to these employment and financial risks. Families often have to shoulder responsibility Over the past two decades, some states have begun to address these gaps. California, New Jersey and about a dozen other states, for example, have launched paid family leave programs. In New York and some other states Medicaid is compensating family caregivers. Washington state is helping finance long-term care coverage. In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris proposed expanding Medicare to cover more in-home assistance, an approach that would have addressed one of the main gaps in the current system. The Democratic presidential nominee’s proposal never moved beyond the campaign trail after Harris lost the 2024 election. “Saturday Night Live’s” “Sister” sketch makes light of an uncomfortable family dynamic, but the issue extends well beyond whether brothers and sisters divide responsibilities fairly. Government policies are behind why so much of that responsibility falls on families in the first place. When public programs do not cover the care older adults need, the need does not disappear. The work, and its financial and personal costs, simply shift to someone else. More often than not, that someone is a daughter. Jane Tavares receives funding from the RRF Foundation for Aging. 48a4b14c4a193313: Philadelphia workers who work for a private company with more than 10 employees may be entitled to paid sick leave. andresr/E+ Collection via Getty ImagesWhat do you do when you wake up with a runny nose and a cough? If you work in Philadelphia, you might have the legal right to a paid sick day. There is no federal right to paid sick leave. However, Philadelphia, like a growing number of states and cities nationwide, requires certain employers to provide paid time off when workers get sick. In Philadelphia, these requirements apply to private-sector employers with more than 10 employees. In theory, under these laws, sick workers have time to recover and avoid spreading germs, and they don’t have to choose between a sick day and a paycheck. For immigrant workers, though, it may not be that easy. I study restaurant work, an industry that depends on the labor of people who are foreign-born. Philadelphia’s award-winning dining scene wouldn’t be the same without the creativity and hard work of people from countries such as Mexico, Honduras and Guatemala. I studied this industry during the COVID-19 pandemic by working in a restaurant from 2021 to 2022, as well as by interviewing restaurant workers, managers and owners from 2021 to 2024. Some interviews were also conducted by my then-fellow Temple University graduate students Andrew Chelius and Camila Franco Rodríguez. Philadelphia’s paid sick leave law has been around since 2015. During the COVID-19 pandemic, federal and local laws temporarily expanded those protections. The Families First Coronavirus Response Act, a federal law which was passed on March 18, 2020, and amended by the CARES Act later that same month, required private-sector employers with less than 500 employees to provide 80 hours of paid sick time each year, on top of their existing paid leave policies, to full-time employees. A 2022 temporary expansion of the local paid sick leave law in Philadelphia, meanwhile, required private-sector employers with 25 or more employees to provide 40 hours of additional paid sick leave to eligible employees. What I found, though, was that several factors could make it hard for workers to take advantage of these policies. Immigrant workers faced unique, additional barriers. ‘$300 for a simple flu’ Our interviews and my immersion in restaurant work showed me that even during a pandemic, restaurant workers had to deal with employers skirting the law or misunderstanding policies. Workers were also impacted by long-standing service industry norms that discourage calling in sick, even when they’re under the weather. Many bosses required doctor’s notes, too, before they paid out any sick time – as I heard from bosses themselves. The local law says, however, that employers may require “reasonable documentation” – but only after an absence of more than two days. Immigrant workers, meanwhile, experienced additional hurdles. Take the example of doctor’s notes. Seeing a doctor is more affordable when you have health insurance. If you’re an undocumented immigrant, getting health insurance is difficult and expensive. Undocumented people are not eligible for Medicaid and are excluded from the Affordable Care Act marketplace. Only a few states try to mend the gap by offering health insurance for low-income people ineligible for Medicaid. Pennsylvania is not one of them. Bill – a pseudonym, like the other participants’ names in this article – is originally from Mexico, and he was a server at an Italian restaurant in Philadelphia’s Center City during the pandemic. When he got sick, his attitude was: “Keep the money. Don’t pay me for sick days.” What kept Bill from claiming sick pay? His employer required him to turn in a doctor’s note before he could receive paid sick leave. However, Bill was undocumented and did not have health insurance. “I wasn’t going to go to the doctor and spend US$300-$400 for a simple flu,” he said. Gaps arise when restaurants have different policies for front-of-house workers, who interact with customers, than back-of-house workers, who staff the kitchen. Willie B. Thomas/DigitalVision Collection via Getty Images Different policies for back-of-house workers In the restaurant where I worked, meanwhile, it was harder for immigrant workers to get sick days than nonimmigrant workers, based on my observations and interviews. This was not necessarily due to ill will toward immigrant workers. But there was a stricter policy around paid sick leave in the kitchen, which was staffed mostly by immigrants from Latin America. The chef who managed the kitchen described his policy like this: “If you bring me proof that you went to the doctor, and the doctor gave you a day or two days of rest, OK, that’s fine.” Those days would be paid. In the customer-facing front of the house, though, where a different manager was in charge, workers – including me – weren’t told they needed proof. These workers were almost all nonimmigrants and mostly white. I heard from Socorro, a prep cook who worked at a different restaurant, that managers where she worked were stingier with sick days for kitchen workers than for servers. “The servers were given their sick leave days and paid them. They’d say, ‘Oh no, my head hurts. I’m not going to work.’ But we couldn’t. ‘Oh, your head hurts? You have to put up with it and come to work.” In that workplace, Socorro said, immigrants also mainly worked in the kitchen, while servers were mostly U.S.-born. Fear of retaliation Immigrant workers in Philadelphia restaurants – both those with and without legal status – also weighed the risks they could face if they asked for paid sick days. These were not risks their nonimmigrant co-workers generally worried about. Claudia, a restaurant worker from Mexico, worked with a local organization called El Comité de Trabajadorxs de Restaurante – the Committee of Restaurant Workers – to educate her peers about paid sick leave. She found that immigrants were really scared of losing their jobs if they spoke up for themselves. “The majority – 80% if not 90% – even if they know they have paid sick hours … they don’t ask for it,” she said. “They don’t claim it, because [they think], ‘Oh, I am an immigrant and they are going to fire me.’ Or, 'Where am I going to get another job?’” Healthy workers, healthy public My research suggests that immigrants in Philadelphia face a gap between the promise and the reality of the city’s paid sick leave policies. These barriers might also help explain gaps in paid sick leave access between foreign-born and U.S.-born workers in other places that require it, like New York City or California. Gaps in access based on immigration status are an equity issue. But beyond that, research suggests that everyone wins if it’s easier for workers to get paid sick leave. Paid sick leave makes for healthier workers, and healthier workers make for a healthier public.
