e853741b74a166f4: Now that Ismail Lasim sudah buat pengakukan terbuka bahawa beliau tidak pernah letak jawatan menteri besar Negeri Sembilan, persoalan penting ialah siapa yang mengutus ‘surat peletakan jawatannya’ kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan?
Persoalan ini amat penting kerana pada hemat saya pihak yang mengutus surat itu telah membohongi atau cuba membohongi Tuanku Muhriz Tuan Munawir.
Apa tidaknya kerana pihak itu telah memaklumkan perkara yang nampaknya tidak benar dan mahu baginda mempercayai isi kandungan surat itu mengenai peletakan jawatan menteri besar.

Orang atau orang-orang yang terlibat dengan penghantaran surat itu saya kira tidak sangka akan reaksi Yang Dipertuan Besar sebaik menerima surat itu. Atas kebijaksanaan Tuanku Muhriz, Istana Negeri Sembilan menegaskan (ketika itu) belum mengesahkan ketulenan surat itu meskipun menurut Setiausaha Agung BN Zambry Abdul Kadir ia telah ditandatangani Ismail.
Sebelum berbicara lanjut elok kita imbau kembali kenyataan Pengelola Bijaya Diraja Istana Negeri Sembilan Azizi Mohamad Ali yang dikeluarkan 17 Nov lalu berbunyi begini:
“Istana Negeri Sembilan mengambil maklum akan kenyataan Zambry Abdul Kadir, Setiausaha Agung Barisan Nasional berhubung peletakan jawatan Ismail Lasim sebagai menteri besar Negeri Sembilan.
Kenyataan itu dimuat naik di media sosial pada 10 malam 16 Nov dan kelihatan berdasarkan salinan surat peletakan jawatan yang berada dalam milikan beliau.
Surat peletakan itu telah dihantar ke Istana Hingap Seremban pada 12.16 pagi 17 November”.

Bagi saya ini amat janggal. Zambry telah menghebahkan ‘peletakan jawatan’ Ismail pada malam 16 Nov tetapi ‘surat peletakan jawatan’ Ismail dihantar ke Istana Hinggap hanya pada keesokan hari yakni 17 Nov.
Bukankah ini bermakna Zambry sudah mengumumkan peletakan jawatan Ismail long before Yang Dipertuan Besar dimaklumkan? Is this proper dalam urusan dengan istana?

Berbalik kenyataan Pengelola Bijya Diraja Istana Negeri Sembilan yang disebut tadi: “Surat itu diserahkan oleh seorang individu yang memperkenalkan dirinya sebagai Hamidi daripada firma guaman Shahrul Hamidi & Haziq"
Aneh. Jika saya mahu letak jawatan misalnya daripada syarikat tempat saya bekerja, saya akan umum sendiri my resignation. Bukan orang lain yang umum.
Dan surat peletakan jawatan akan saya serah sendiri kepada majikan bukan meminta pihak lain melakukannya.
Dalam kes ‘peletakan jawatan’ Ismail adakah ‘molek’ menyerahkan surat kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar menerusi third party? Dan tidak menghadap untuk mempersembahkan surat personally?

Ada lagi yang dihuraikan Pengelola Bijaya Diraja Istana Negeri Sembilan. Menurut beliau: “Pada jam 6.38 petang,semalam (16 Nov 2026 ) Setiausaha Sulit Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan telah menyampaikan kepada Ismail melalui aplikasi WhatsApp perkenan Tuanku Muhriz untuk menghadap seperti yang dipohon oleh menteri besar itu.
Perkara tu telah diakui terima oleh Ismail dan acara menghadap telah ditetapkan pada pukul 10 pagi Jumaat (20 Nov).
Perkenan untuk menghadap itu telah diberikan 80 minit lebih awal sebelum siaran media Zambry yang memaklumkan peletakan jawatan itu.
Aneh dan pelik. Ismail yang memohon menghadap bertindak ‘meneruskan hasrat letak jawatan’ (yang diumum Zambry) setelah tahu Yang Dipertuan Besar telah perkenankan permohonannya?

Berbalik pula kepada kenyataan setiausaha agung BN itu. Kata Zambry pengerusi gabungan itu Zahid Hamidi sudah menerima salinan suara peletakan jawatan Ismail yang diutuskan kepada Yang Dipertuan Besar.

“Pengerusi Barisan Nasional akan mengemukakan cadangan calon menteri besar yang baharu untuk dipersembahkan ke hadapan Duli Yang Maha Mulia Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilsn selaras dengan peruntukan Undang Undang Tubuh Kerajaan Negeri Sembilan”.

Zahid insisted Ismail resigned voluntarily. Beliau juga memberitahu media hanya satu nama akan dipersembahkan. Ini menurut saya tidak beri Yang Dipertuan Besar banyak pilihan. Atau tidak beri pilihan langsung.

Apa pun itu sudah tidak terpakai kerana hari ini Yang Dipertuan Besar bertitah supaya Ismail teruskan tugas sebagai menteri besar. Ini kata Ismail pada sidang medianya selepas menghadap Tuanku Muhriz.
Saya ulangi apa kata Ismail pada sidang media itu “Saya tak pernah setuju surat ini dihantar dan saya pun tak hantar sendiri surat ini kepada Tuanku. Saya hanya tahu melalui media sosial.”
Namun Ismail mengaku surat peletakan jawatan semenagnya ada dalam simpanan pimpinan parti namun tidak dinyatakan sebabnya.
Setahu saya ada parti mewajibkan Ahli Parlimen dan Adun yang mewaklinya menandatangnai surat melepaskan jawatan atau kedudukan dalam usaha memastkan mereka tidak lompat parti.
The pre signed resignation letter will be released in the event of crossing over to other parties. Ini amalan lazim sebelum ada anti hopping law.
Bagaimanapun boleh dirumuskan penjelasan Ismail diterima Yang Dipertuan Besar pada upacara menghadap semalam. Lantas baginda mahu Ismail kekal sebagai menteri besar.
Bagi saya episod Negeri Sembilan tamparan hebat kepada BN khususnya Umno yang selama ini megah mendakwa ia mempertahakan Raja-Raja Melayu dn kedaulatan Istana.
Di Negeri Sembilan tidak boleh dinafikan Umno mendekati (bersekongkol?) kumpulan yang cuba menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz daripada takhta dan gagal.
Kesimpulan terbaik saya kira dibuat oleh Naib Pengerusi DAP Syahredzan Johan “Semua tindakan ini adalah berasaskan suatu perkara yang terbukti tidak benar. Ismail Lasim tidak pernah letak jawatan.”
Adakah Umno cuba untuk memperdayakan Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan dan rakyat dalam hal ini?
Nota kaki: Terbaharu, lewat petang ini Azizi mengeluarkan kenyatan menyatakan Ismail perlu menunjukkan beliau mendapat sokongan majoriti Adun untuk terus memegang jawatan menteri besar.
Kenyataan itu juga berkata tidak tepat dan tidak berdasarkan fakta untuk mengatakan Istana mahu Ismail kekal sebagai menteri besar memandangkan beliau sendiri menegaskan tidak meletakkan jawatan.
Menurutnya, pihak Istana akan mematuhi sepenuhnya konvensyen dan peruntukan perlembagaan.

2b876ce610b840bc: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
What we learned when our Roundtables explored the quest to make minds immortal

To preserve our sense of self, some scientists are working on ways to keep our brains going—even beyond death. In their quest for cognitive immortality, these “mind savers” are exploring everything from head transplants and brain freezing to conscious software avatars.

In the latest MIT Technology Review Roundtables event, senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado joined science editor Mary Beth Griggs to examine these ideas. After following the money, the science, and the philosophy, he came back part skeptical, part awestruck. Here’s a taste of what Antonio found—and what he made of it.

Not all the projects are quite what they seem: A $190 million US government program to develop replacement brain tissue is officially about treating stroke, but “it’s also a fig leaf for the actual ambition”: living forever.

AI could lead to convincing mind clones: Large language models are making it possible to build AI copies of people that act quite like the real thing. “This digital avatar might not be good enough for you, but what if it’s good enough for me?”
Immortality can be a hard sell: One company, Nectome, wants to preserve brains within 12 minutes of medically assisted death. “If you’re selling a hot product, this is not it.”
It’s not always clear what we’re trying to preserve: “I’m not even sure that I have a very good claim to be myself.”
There’s an upside to life as a brain in a jar: “You can surf the internet. I do that pretty much 12 hours a day, anyway.”
To find out which of these ideas might actually work, subscribers can now watch the full conversation on demand.

c1cb73c3d8571045: From Kua Kia Soong
The controversy over the RM1,000 land premium for the 99-year lease renewal of the Kuala Lumpur and Selangor Chinese Assembly Hall (KLSCAH) has become another occasion for racial politicking.
Some have portrayed the decision as an unjustified privilege for a Chinese organisation, while others have defended it as a concession to the Chinese community.
Both sides are missing the bigger issue: whether Malaysia genuinely respects its historical and cultural heritage or allows commercial development and political expediency to take precedence.

Established in 1923, KLSCAH is more than a Chinese communal building. It has played an important role in Kuala Lumpur's political, social and cultural history and has been used by Malaysians of different ethnic groups and political affiliations.
Its significance should be assessed in the context of national history, rather than reduced to the racial identity of its users.

The controversy also raises a more fundamental question: why is the preservation of historical buildings and cultural institutions in Malaysia so often treated as an inconvenience rather than a public responsibility?
Monorail and disregard for historical landmarks
Consider the fate of Kuala Lumpur's historic temples.

The Guan Yin temple, established in the 1890s or possibly earlier, is one of the city's historic places of worship. Located beside the Maharajalela Monorail station, its historical setting and architectural character are overshadowed by the surrounding concrete infrastructure.
The temple has survived fires, Kuala Lumpur's transformation and generations of change. Yet how much consideration was given to its historical setting when the monorail infrastructure was introduced?
Modern public transport is undoubtedly necessary. But must modernisation mean historical buildings are reduced to insignificant structures dwarfed by concrete and steel?
This is not an argument against public transport, but for intelligent urban planning that allows modern infrastructure and historical landmarks to coexist.
The Sydney Monorail, for instance, was decommissioned in 2013 and dismantled in 2014 as part of the city's transition to light rail.
Another new development now threatens the Guan Yin temple. The authorities should assess its impact on the historic precinct before any damage becomes irreversible.
The wider Chinese community should also be asking why more has not been done to protect such landmarks.
Kuala Lumpur is destroying its own history
The fate of other historical buildings in Kuala Lumpur should prompt reflection on our priorities.
Pudu Jail, built in 1895, was once among the city's most recognisable landmarks. Its imposing walls and famous mural formed part of Kuala Lumpur's physical and social history.
The prison complex was demolished in stages, with most of the buildings gone by 2012. Only sections of its exterior wall and entrance were retained.

Whatever one's views on the colonial prison system, Pudu Jail was part of our history. Its preservation could have provided an important historical and educational site. Instead, most of it disappeared.
Then there was Bok House, a neo-classical mansion built in 1929 by businessman Chua Cheng Bok along Jalan Ampang. It also housed the well-known restaurant Le Coq d'Or.

Despite appeals by heritage advocates, the mansion was demolished in 2006. The argument that it lacked sufficient historical value illustrated how little importance was attached to architectural heritage.
The Cathay cinema, another familiar Kuala Lumpur landmark, also disappeared in the name of urban redevelopment.
How many more buildings must we lose before we realise that a city is not defined merely by its shopping malls, luxury condominiums and skyscrapers?
The Sultan Abdul Samad Building, Central Market and historic buildings around Dataran Merdeka have fortunately survived.
But their survival should not be an excuse for complacency. They require continued conservation, proper maintenance and protection from insensitive development.
Malaysia's collective memory under threat
This is not simply a Chinese community issue.

Malaysia's heritage includes Malay villages, traditional wooden houses, mosques, Indian temples, colonial buildings, indigenous settlements, archaeological sites, historic cemeteries and natural landscapes.

The demolition of the Sri Uchimalai Muniswarar Temple in Rawang in February was another painful reminder of the vulnerability of places of worship with longstanding community ties. The temple was demolished after the landowner sought possession of the site.

The controversy over the 130-year-old Dewi Sri Pathrakaliamman Temple on Jalan Masjid India, Kuala Lumpur, also raised fundamental questions about how development should accommodate historic places of worship.

Although the authorities subsequently identified a replacement site, the episode showed how vulnerable such institutions can be when land ownership and development interests take precedence over historical continuity.

We should also remember the traditional Malay kampungs lost to urban redevelopment, indigenous communities displaced by development projects and historic landscapes sacrificed to commercial interests.
The heritage of the Orang Asli and indigenous peoples of Sabah and Sarawak deserves the same protection as Kuala Lumpur's old temples and shophouses.
A nation that remembers only the history of its politically powerful communities has a distorted understanding of itself.

Developers should be required to assess the historical, cultural and social significance of buildings and places of worship before obtaining development approvals. Where possible, they should preserve these sites in their original locations rather than treating relocation as the default solution.

In the latest KLSCAH controversy, critics who believe public institutions should not receive special consideration for heritage preservation must explain why the same principle should not apply to every other historic building, temple, mosque, church, traditional settlement and cultural institution in Malaysia.

Should a historic Malay institution be required to pay commercial land premiums even when its land is designated for institutional use? Should an Indian temple be denied consideration simply because its preservation benefits a particular religious community?
We must reject this absurd racial arithmetic.
The question is not whether KLSCAH is Chinese, Malay or Indian. It is whether the institution has historical, cultural and public significance that deserves protection.
Kua Kia Soong is a former MP and a former director of Suaram.

b7f674ad7efc71b2: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence giant behind Claude, has just pulled off the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history. The company raised US$81 billion by listing on the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market, beating the previous all-time record of US$75 billion set by SpaceX earlier this year. Initially set at $US83, Anthropic’s share price soared to US$111 after its debut, briefly nudging the company’s value past US$2 trillion, before falling again as investors took profits. The blockbuster stock market listing comes at a nervous moment in the AI sector. Investors are increasingly questioning whether the huge sums of money being poured into the AI boom are justified, and many are reducing their exposure to technology stocks. Adding to this shakiness has been the shock departure of chipmaker Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, following an affair scandal. Anthropic’s debut certainly sets a benchmark for rival OpenAI, which still plans to go public. But we shouldn’t mistake investor enthusiasm in one company for a broader vote of confidence in the global AI industry. What does Anthropic’s performance tell us? One thing we can learn from this week’s result is that there is a huge amount of demand for Anthropic itself. Strong revenue was one factor. At the end of October, Anthropic’s annualised revenue run rate (an estimate of yearly revenue based on the previous month) was US$81 billion. But the company’s popularity likely also played a role. Claude is one of the most widely used AI tools around the globe. “Familiarity bias” is a well known phenomenon in investing. Intense demand meant many smaller investors missed out on getting shares ahead of the official listing. Last week, Bloomberg reported the share offering was about six times oversubscribed. According to the Wall Street Journal, only about 15% of available shares were ultimately allocated to retail investors. Is Anthropic’s huge valuation justified? Anthropic’s share price closed the day at US$97.17, up 17% from its IPO price, which values the company at US$1.76 trillion. That’s slightly less than where SpaceX landed at the end of its first day, at US$2.1 trillion. But it’s still a colossal figure, even accounting for the fact that Anthropic beat OpenAI to generating a quarterly operating profit earlier this year (before returning to an operating loss the following quarter). For Anthropic, like any company, going public should make it easier to raise large amounts of capital. That could be important for a company which has already made about US$900 billion in future spending commitments – mostly on computing infrastructure – between now and 2045. However, it’s important to look at how these commitments play out in the short and long term. About half of this spending is due by 2030. The near-term bill over the next 12 months is about US$70 billion, which is manageable with its current revenue run rate of US$81 billion. Other concerns may be more pressing. Anthropic’s third-quarter revenue rose 47% – which is strong – but this compares to a growth rate of 144% in the second quarter. This suggests a sharp slowdown in growth overall. Token prices have also been falling, driven in part by more competition from cheaper AI models. Also on revenue, the company has warned that some of its customers – “particularly early-stage and high-growth companies” – rely on external financing. This could reduce their spending with Anthropic if that financing dries up. What to watch after this public listing For any company, listing on a public stock exchange introduces much more scrutiny. Previously, the focus on Anthropic has centred on its technology and growth potential. Now, there’ll be a renewed focus on corporate governance. Beyond the financial metrics of revenue growth, profitability, cash flow and more, investors will now more closely scrutinise how management balances commercial returns with AI safety, privacy and social responsibility. Speaking just before the Nasdaq listing, Chief Executive Dario Amodei acknowledged people’s serious safety concerns: We have always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or nation states, to economic disruption, to losing control of AI systems. But he expressed faith in Anthropic’s ability to get the balance right: If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. Protesters staged major rallies outside the Nasdaq exchange’s New York headquarters and outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters. They called for stronger government regulation and a slowdown or total pause on AI development. What does this mean for rival OpenAI? Another of the world’s major AI companies, OpenAI, had initially planned its own public listing this year. However, it has now ruled this out until 2027, citing safety concerns around the technology. Anthropic’s IPO creates both opportunities and challenges for its rival. On the plus side, Anthropic’s performance gives OpenAI and potential investors a yardstick – including financial performance benchmarks and lots of other useful information. But now that Anthropic has become a publicly listed company, this industry is about to come under even more intense scrutiny. If public sentiment about AI worsens between now and when OpenAI launches its IPO, it could pay a steep price. b00d2094481c93e7: Now that the Melaka state election is done and dusted, here are six harsh truths Malaysians need to confront.
The first is this: like it or not, the Barisan Nasional (BN)-Perikatan Nasional (PN) bloc won resoundingly.
There is no other way to describe it.
Many of the majorities recorded were astronomical, suggesting that Malay voters remain firmly behind these two coalitions, particularly Umno and PAS.
The prospect of BN and PN forming the next federal government, aided by voter transference between the two coalitions, appears increasingly likely with each passing day.
The second harsh truth is one we are often reluctant to acknowledge: many Malay voters appear largely indifferent to corruption.
The Tabung Haji and Felda controversies associated with Umno barely registered at the polls and did little to dent the party's support.

Meanwhile, PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang, who commands considerable influence among the religious electorate, continues to advance the narrative of Malay-Muslim political dominance with relatively little challenge.
It is a simple yet powerful message. The idea that Malay-Muslims must remain in power is easy to understand and sell.

Against such populist narratives, the Madani government's successes in attracting investments, creating jobs and improving fiscal management have struggled to gain traction, even when the achievements of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's administration were communicated effectively.
The third harsh truth is for a specific group of Malaysians: those in Bersama.
Twice now, despite their hard work, sincerity and idealism, they have come away empty-handed.
Bersama may yet have something to learn from Umno and PAS and their marriage of convenience.
The relationship between the two parties is far from a fairy-tale partnership. I suspect there remains deep distrust between them. After all, what became of Muafakat Nasional?
Nevertheless, both parties recognised that cooperation was necessary for political survival.

Rafizi Ramli may have serious differences with Anwar, but if the PKR president was once able to set aside his differences with mentor-turned-nemesis Dr Mahathir Mohamad to wrest Putrajaya from BN's iron grip in 2018, why can't Rafizi do the same?

There is also a reason figures such as Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, Mahathir, Hadi and Anwar have remained relevant for decades. Rather than dismissing them as political dinosaurs, Bersama might do well to study the lessons they offer.
The fourth harsh lesson is for PKR itself.
The time has come for Anwar to do something bold if the party hopes to survive the next general election.
He must begin laying the groundwork for a new generation of leaders and gradually step back from centre stage.
Unless fresh faces are given room to emerge, public enthusiasm for PKR may continue to fade.
There is little point talking about a second term for Anwar and his administration if the party remains unwilling to reinvent itself.
The fifth lesson is that Pakatan Harapan must strike meaningful deals with the ruling coalitions in Sabah and Sarawak.
Those arrangements must go beyond simply addressing demands under the Malaysia Agreement 1963.
Anwar still possesses something neither BN nor PN is likely to offer: the possibility of an East Malaysian prime minister.
Such a commitment could fundamentally reshape the political landscape.
The sixth and final harsh lesson concerns voter turnout.
During the Melaka election, it was reported that about 80% of Malay voters turned out, compared with only 60% of Chinese voters.
Overall turnout stood at 70%.
If Malaysia is to chart a different course, every vote matters. An 85% turnout, especially if it includes stronger participation from non-Malay voters, could significantly alter electoral outcomes.
I hope the Election Commission will make every effort to help the roughly one million Malaysians living overseas cast their ballots wherever they reside.
The higher the voter turnout, the greater the chance that Malaysia's future will be determined by the broadest possible expression of its people's will.
We are heading into stormy waters. We need to be honest with ourselves if we are to avoid the maelstrom that could engulf us all.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
b9181880dad68760: The last few weeks haven’t been good for the US tech industry. The recent US midterms elections signalled strong pushbacks against AI, data centres and big tech in general. Then there’s last week’s breakdown of Microsoft services followed almost immediately by an outage that grounded civilian flights across the US for hours.

Donald Trump's aggressive policies in his second presidency – tariffs, embargoes, sanctions and even military actions against many countries including those once considered allies – are beginning to register loudly in the risk assessments of many countries. The latest incidents bring even more intense focus on this matter.

China was the first to face US actions on its tech sector, especially those involving semiconductors, software and AI. However, China has the resources to deal with this. Chinese companies such as Huawei and DeepSeek are successfully overcoming these obstacles and showing they’re good at converting these problems into opportunities.

Europe is a bit late to the party, taking longer to realise they aren’t high on the US list of friends and allies any more. The inertia and in-fighting in its huge coalition of disparate European nations slowed things down a lot. But even there the logjam is breaking.

A particular shock was Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The Trump administration's overt siding with Russian president Vladimir Putin is unnerving Russia’s European neighbours. They realise they depend too much on the US, whether for office productivity tools, weapons, satellite capabilities or semiconductor chips that power their AI ambitions.
A wake-up call

The recent incidents where SpaceX withheld its Starlink and Starshield services to Ukraine’s war efforts are wake-up calls on the perils of depending too much on an increasingly unreliable partner. The same goes with the repeated US threats of annexation of Canada, Greenland, Panama as well as the de facto annexation of Venezuela.
There’s a growing international desire to reduce dependence on US technology, especially critical ones for defence, finance and businesses.

That we can have service breakdowns such at Microsoft and at the US Federal Aviation Administration shatter the decades-old illusions of the superiority, invincibility and desirability of American technology.

Now Malaysia is not China. We don’t have the resources to build cutting-edge tech we can use for ourselves and perhaps sell to the world. But neither do most countries out there,for that matter. We still have to rely on external technologies and services for many areas, even critical ones.
But change must happen. While we’re good at producing everything from agricultural commodities to manufactured goods, we have never been known for being particularly technologically innovative.

But given Asean’s 700 million people and over US$4.5 trillion in GDP, and given the need for economic and security blocs to deal with aggressive and even predatory superpowers, we have the ability, resources and motivation to achieve our goals.

That the overheating global AI markets could crash has been on everybody’s mind lately. Recent events, such as grave warnings about the potential dangers of AI going rogue and harming humanity, coming from AI's biggest boosters themselves, as well as scandals and personnel changes that can potentially alter the tech landscape, may accelerate such an economic scenario.

What’s not on anybody’s bingo cards, however, were the Microsoft and FAA outages. They reveal the dangers of both transitioning complex current systems to new technologies as well as concentrating it in the hands of a handful of American tech giants so much of the computing power that the world needs.
Computing as a service

Over the past few decades the world had increasingly relied on computing hardware and software being made available on subscription from remote data centres owned and operated by mostly US tech giants. Such “cloud computing” means users rent computing services rather than owning the hardware and software themselves. They’ve become tenants rather than landlords, and their landlords have a near-monopoly.

We are seeing the perils of being tied to massive, remote cloud computing capabilities, as when Ukraine and Iran bombed some of Russia’s and the US’s data centres. We’ve always thought having giant tech companies offering capital, expertise and multiple redundancies would guarantee us from those dreaded “single points of failure”.

We were wrong. We are now seeing how single points of failure can and do indeed fail and shut things down. And the human part of the deal – a president or a CEO – can actually be that single point of failure and cause havoc such as we’ve never planned for or insured against.

Another lesson over the recent past has been that middle powers – such as Ukraine and Iran – that had their backs against the wall can show amazing resilience and innovation. They are both successfully holding back global superpowers, lobbing actual bombs and missiles at them, and even bloodying up some noses in return.

There are no reasons that Malaysia, already a reasonably-sized economic middle power, can’t create the tech and infrastructures that can provide us with some sovereignty and hence protection against hostile nations. If Malaysia is to be Boleh at anything, this is certainly an area where we must Boleh.

Meanwhile, I came across a wonderful term used to describe the ability of some systems to degrade under attack but still provide some reduced, predictable functionality, rather than totally collapsing like what happened at Microsoft and the FAA. It's called graceful degradation, a term I wished I’d invented to describe myself growing old.
I'm degrading for sure, with the occasional outage, though whether it's graceful or not still remains to be seen!
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
b9b68b51845fc3b9: Japan is yet to establish the Human Rights Protection Bill and a independent national human rights institution
Originally published on Global Voices
Anti-immigration policy protest in Oct 2026. Screen capture from the Japan Unfiltered YouTube Channel. Fair Use

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.
A newborn Black baby delivered at a clinic in Tokyo’s Meguro Ward became the target of a barrage of racist harassment online.

The clinic published the baby’s photo with a congratulatory message on its social media account as part of its routine “babies born this month” photo series. A screenshot of the post spread widely on X, gaining more than 1.3 million views within a day. The post attracted many hateful comments loaded with anti-immigrant sentiment and racial discrimination against non-white and non-Japanese people. Some of the hateful comments received thousands of likes.
All comments have since been removed from the post, and the clinic has disabled commenting on its Instagram.

This incident sheds light on two issues within Japanese society. On one level, it reflects how racist hate speech still remains rampant in Japan. But more broadly, it exposes a missing layer of justice infrastructure: Japan has no independent human rights commission empowered to handle discrimination complaints, no enforceable national hate speech law, and no effective way to force platforms to remove hate speech targeting entire groups.

While some cultural critics argue that the widespread racial discrimination in Japan stems from the younger generation’s inadequate interest in foreign cultures and development, others argue that the prevalence of online hate speech is to a large extent related to a lack of effective domestic legislation and human rights education.

Despite being a signatory to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD) since 1995, Japan has not passed the Human Rights Protection Bill or established an independent national human rights institution to investigate human rights violations and penalize perpetrators. While there have been numerous attempts to pass such a bill, it was tabled multiple times in the 2000s and early 2010s. Critics say the efforts failed because the public feared it could violate the freedom of speech protected by the Constitution.
Toothless anti-discrimination national laws

Thus, instead of passing a comprehensive set of laws, it addresses discrimination and human rights through issue-specific laws, such as the Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Human Rights Awareness-Raising (2000), the Act for Eliminating Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (2013), the Act on the Promotion of Efforts to Eliminate Unfair Discriminatory Speech and Behavior against Persons with Countries of Origin other than Japan (2016), the Act on the Promotion of the Elimination of Buraku Discrimination (2016), as well as the Act on the Promotion of Public Understanding of the Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (2023), which aim to raise public awareness about human rights and providing government support rather than criminalizing hate speech and discrimination.

For example, while the Hate Speech Elimination Act was enacted to curb xenophobic street rallies that terrify ethnic minorities residing in Japan, such as the series of protests against Kyoto Korean Elementary School between December 2009 and March 2010, it does not declare hate speech illegal, nor penalize offenders with fines or jail sentences.

Moreover, the law only protects foreigners with a legal status, but excludes undocumented migrants, asylum seekers, and Indigenous peoples, including the Ainu and Ryūkyūans. The law’s legal scope is at odds with the United Nations’ recommendations, which state that a signatory of the ICERD must “ensure legislative guarantees against racial discrimination apply to non-citizens regardless of their immigration status, and that the implementation of legislation does not have a discriminatory effect on non-citizens.” Legal experts have criticized the restrictive clause of the law for, as Shuji Oda, president of the Dai-Ichi Tokyo Bar Association, says, “giving rise to a false reverse implication that hate speech directed at individuals without legal residency status is permissible.”

The toothless anti-discrimination laws only manage to contain explicit discriminatory actions against disabled people, Burakumin (feudal outcasts), LGBTQ+ people, and foreigners with legal status; they have not eliminated hate speech. Meanwhile, street rallies against immigrant and imported labor have surged amid stagnant local wages, inflation, and rising living costs. Though these protests are usually small in scale, they attract a large number of social media comments, with plenty of discriminatory remarks and hate speech against foreigners.

Additionally, none of the aforementioned laws has a mechanism to force internet platforms to remove harmful content; this results in the spread of xenophobia, homophobia, hatred against social minorities, and a racist online culture.
Kawasaki model

As Japanese national politics has stalled the enactment of the Human Rights Protection Bill, some local governments have started building the legal framework from the bottom up to address local unrest targeting ethnic minorities.

Kawasaki City, which is home to a large Zainichi Korean population in Kanagawa Prefecture, was the first municipality in Japan to introduce punitive local laws to curb protests that “injure the human dignity of others,” as described by the city’s Justice Department.

Since the national Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Awareness was passed in 2000, the city enacted its own Children’s Rights Ordinance in 2000 and Human Rights Ombudsperson Ordinance in 2001, which paved the way for the establishment of a local independent Human Rights Ombudsperson system for receiving and investigating complaints on bullying, abuse, and discrimination.

Following a surge of demonstrations calling for the exclusion of people of foreign origin around 2013, the city enacted the Ordinance for the Creation of a City that Respects Human Rights and is Free from Discrimination in December 2019, which prohibits discrimination based on race, nationality, ethnic origin, gender, sexual orientation, and disability. The ordinance also bans using loudspeakers, placards, or flyers that induce hatred against people originating from outside Japan and their descendants. Under the Ordinance, repeat offenders would have their identities publicly disclosed, and they could be fined up to JPY 500,000 (approximately USD 3,130). The city would also keep a record of hate groups and ban them from using public facilities, such as sports venues and parks.

Furthermore, the ordinance established an expert panel empowered to review hate speech and instruct online platforms to remove extreme content targeting a specific group of people and disclose the abusers’ identities.

While the ordinance has managed to reduce discriminatory protests against Korean-Japanese communities within Kawasaki City, it is powerless when the protests take place in neighboring jurisdictions. Moreover, thus far the criminal penalty of the local ordinance just punishes abusers targeting people originating from outside of Japan; LGBTQ+, disabled, and indigenous communities have remained unprotected. It cannot penalize landlords or employers who discriminate and has limited power over online abuse, as internet companies are not legally bound by local laws.
Human rights education translated into moral education

Various UN bodies have repeatedly criticized Japan for failing to enact a comprehensive anti-discrimination law and establish an independent commission to investigate and prosecute abusers in line with the “Paris Principle,” the official international standards for national human rights institutions. Yet, to date, Japanese society still lacks the consensus and determination to pass the Human Rights Protection Bill.
While proponents of stalling the legislation cite potential violations of free speech, a deeper reason relates to local xenophobia and perceptions of human rights.

The concept of human rights was introduced to Japan about 150 years ago, during the Japanese modernization period beginning in the late Edo and early Meiji era. However, when the Constitution of the Empire of Japan was promulgated in 1889, it defined citizens’ rights not as inherent human rights, but as “rights of subjects” granted by the Emperor.

Only after World War II was the concept of universal human rights re-introduced and localized to criticize Japan’s wartime militarization of society and crimes against non-Japanese people. Yet, human rights education in schools is often confused with conventional moral education, which emphasizes individual responsibility to family, society, and the country, and the need to maintain harmonious human relations through interpersonal politeness and consideration.

However, the individual morality approach overlooks the structural causes of discrimination and fails to empower individuals as rights-holders to address the problem of systematic discrimination, as pointed out by a group of Japanese teachers from the Institute of Global Education and Culture in a proposal to better integrate moral and human rights education in 2014:
日本では人権教育・啓発の場で「おもいやり」「やさしさ」などが強調される一方で、権利そのものを学習することは低調である。[…]
[…]具体的な「権利」という側面も、また「社会的に」問題を解決しようという側面も極めて弱い。「思いやり」を強調する抽象的・心情主義的教育は、私的な人間関係の中での問題解決ばかりを強調し、権利を具体的に考え実現しようとする力をむしろ弱めているといえる。
In Japan, human rights education and awareness-raising campaigns have kept emphasising concepts like ‘consideration for others’ (omoi-yari) and ‘kindness’ while downplaying education on rights. […]

It’s extremely weak in addressing different aspects of individual rights and the social resolution of rights-related problems. The emphasis on ‘understanding’ is both abstract and sentimental; as such, education relies solely on problem-solving within private interpersonal relationships and will hence weaken the ability to think concretely about rights and exercising one’s rights.

Earlier this year, Human Rights Watch urged the newly elected prime minister Sanae Takaichi to legislate a comprehensive anti-discrimination law and create an independent national human rights body to address the rise of xenophobic sentiments against immigrants. Although the right-leaning government has no intention of resurrecting the Human Rights Protection Bill, a civic coalition has formed to advocate for an independent National Human Rights Institution with investigative and corrective powers to address discrimination and human rights abuses by 2028.
Written by Jo Carter
023c96572d69f0f2: It has to be Anfield, of all places. The fixture list is up to its wicked tricks again.
Just as it did for Manchester City after the guilty verdict was announced, Sunday’s big game sees United go to that simmering cauldron of hostility at a critical moment in their history.
Mauricio Pochettino takes charge, fresh from guiding the USA to an 8-0 aggregate win over Haiti in the Concacaf Nations League.
From Haiti to hate, you might say, and instead of just 24,000 at Cincinnati’s TQL Stadium, the world and a good chunk of the universe will be watching.
But is Anfield still the forbidding fortress it is cracked up to be?
We know what happened with City, who ran out comfortable winners after two harsh yellow cards gave them a man advantage.
But it’s not just star-studded City we’re talking about: only Crystal Palace, who are bottom, and Nottingham Forest (16th) have worse home records than Liverpool.
A paltry five points is all the Reds have mustered from five games despite the wall of sound that is supposed to make opponents weak at the knees.
They have played all three teams above them in the table, but it is only due to having the best away record that they sit in fourth place.
Even more relevant, though, is that United do not seem intimidated by the place.
Indeed, the Devils have a good record here despite Liverpool’s recent overall superiority.
Kopites may still think fondly of the 7-0 annihilation of 2023, but since then Liverpool haven’t won there in three games, and just once in seven meetings in all competitions.
However, if the Devils have found some steel, Pochettino himself will only have reason to dread the Anfield roar.
The Argentine has won only one game there, and that was when he was at Southampton.
In 19 games against Liverpool in total, with the Saints, Chelsea, and mostly Tottenham, he has won only three times, with five draws and 11 defeats.
At Spurs, he won only once and his greatest disappointment in football was the Champions League final of 2019, when a second-minute penalty distorted the game.
Pochettino had relished the underdog role with Southampton, beating United as well in just his fourth game in charge.
The trick seemed to be making a fast start, which took the big boys by surprise.
After a maximum of three training sessions since landing on Wednesday, the 54-year-old will hardly be able to transform United.
Still jet-lagged, a fast start may be beyond his powers to engineer, but there is no doubt that this will be another occasion where he’ll be the underdog.
Three of his staff did arrive earlier, but it will be expecting an awful lot of the ‘new manager bounce’ to match a Liverpool side that is showing signs of becoming an Andoni Iraola team.
An interesting aspect of Poch’s appointment is that he was not Jim Ratcliffe’s choice, but that of the Glazers, who pulled rank on the minority owner.
CEO Omar Berrada and Football Director Jason Wilcox wanted Eddie Howe but were overruled by the family in Florida, who had been impressed by Pochettino’s stewardship of the American national team.

Ratcliffe has been strangely quiet of late and, with the protests against the owners showing no sign of abating, you wonder if he’ll carry out his promise to walk away should he get the abuse the Glazers endure.
He’s already very close to that level and now he’s been firmly put in his place by the majority owners.
A hedge fund billionaire pal of the Glazers, Ken Griffin, helped to pay Pochettino’s salary at cash-strapped US Soccer.
Even before he crossed the Atlantic, Poch was already talking about signings in the January transfer window.
He’s widely expected to add Folarin Balogun and Antonee Robinson from his US team to fill the gaping holes at striker and left-back.
It will be fascinating to see if United find funds for him that Ratcliffe denied Michael Carrick.
This is not to say that he won’t give everyone a chance at Old Trafford. In the US job, he tried no less than 77 players and unearthed several teenage starlets before honing down his squad.
This augurs well for United’s academy traditions, but it came too late for wonderkid J.J. Gabriel, who has gone to Real Madrid.
Liverpool are also being linked with more recruits to bolster Iraola’s promising first three months.
The Spaniard is more of a slow starter, having gone 10 games before he notched his first win at Bournemouth, but we know the rest.
And there are welcome signs that despite injury disruptions, he’s getting his message across.
He’s certainly more in tune with Jurgen Klopp’s heavy metal than the more patient Arne Slot ever was.
He must feel that the lightning breaks of Bradley Barcola, Cody Gakpo and Victor Munoz could overwhelm a United defence that has been ragged of late.
Indeed, the jitteriness of the back four even spread to Sanne Lemmens in the last game.
And you can’t help but feel that if Florian Wirtz can’t flourish against this defence, he never will cut the mustard in the EPL.
He scored two in Germany’s 5-0 rout of the Netherlands, so he’s primed.
But the focus will inevitably be on the visitors’ dugout to see the new would-be saviour.
He’s already promised to make the players run and ‘unblock’ their brains.
It sounds like he has half a chance, but maybe not on Sunday.

2e71f13f3cdb0ff7: Malaysia’s ports handled 33.07 million 20-foot equivalent units, or TEUs, in 2025. Through September 2026, they had already moved a provisional 25,713,471 TEUs, up 4.8% from the corresponding nine months last year.
That expanding flow of containers provides an encouraging backdrop for everyone whose business depends on moving, storing and delivering goods.
At the centre stands Port Klang.

Its throughput reached 11,804,541 TEUs, growing 5.4% and contributing 45.9% of the national total. More tellingly, Port Klang supplied approximately 50.8% of Malaysia’s additional container volume over the period. It is not merely the largest contributor; it is driving a disproportionate share of national growth.
Already ranked the world’s 10th busiest container port in Lloyd’s List’s 2026 table, based on 2025 throughput, Port Klang is demonstrating why its international standing matters to Malaysia.
More than a transshipment success
Port Klang’s strength lies in the combination of international connectivity and Malaysian gateway trade.

Imports and exports together reached 5,265,991 TEUs, representing 44.6% of throughput. Exports grew 6.2% to 2,625,382 TEUs, while imports increased 4.3% to 2,640,609 TEUs. Combined gateway growth was approximately 5.2%.
These figures measure container activity, not trade value. Nevertheless, they show expanding demand for the port’s services in both directions.
For manufacturers, importers, freight forwarders and warehouse operators, this is the commercially significant story: Port Klang’s growth is not confined to cargo changing ships.
Transshipment also advanced, increasing 5.5% to 6,538,550 TEUs. Its 55.4% share of throughput underlines the gateway’s substantial international connecting role.
Serving Malaysian commerce while connecting global shipping networks gives Port Klang two important foundations for growth.
Two terminals, complementary strengths

Westports remains the anchor, handling 8,546,840 TEUs and contributing 72.4% of Port Klang’s throughput. Its 1.3% overall increase included export growth of 2% and transshipment growth of 2.2%, although imports declined 1.9%.
Its scale remains formidable. Westports handled 68.8% of Port Klang’s gateway cargo and 75.3% of its transshipment business.

Northport, meanwhile, supplied exceptional momentum. Its throughput rose 17.9% to 3,257,701 TEUs, contributing approximately 82% of Port Klang’s additional volume. Imports grew 19.6%, while exports and transshipment volumes increased by 17.7% and 17.1%, respectively.
That breadth deserves recognition. Northport’s gateway cargo reached 1,640,511 TEUs, alongside 1,617,190 TEUs of transshipment. Its progress strengthened both sides of Port Klang’s business.
Westports’ larger base and Northport’s acceleration demonstrate the value of complementary terminal strengths.
Scale backed by capability
Global leadership requires infrastructure that shipping lines can use with confidence.

Westports states that its facilities can accommodate container ships of 24,000 TEUs, supported by a natural deep harbour reaching up to 18 metres. Its expansion programme is expected to increase annual capacity from 14 million to 28 million TEUs.
That is future capacity, not cargo already secured. However, it provides a credible platform for defending Port Klang’s top ten position.
The decisive test will be execution: dependable vessel handling, efficient clearance, productive yards and reliable connections beyond the terminal gate.
A stronger national network
Johor reinforces Malaysia’s maritime weight.

Port of Tanjung Pelepas (PTP) handled 10,973,966 TEUs, up 5.4%, while Johor Port at Pasir Gudang handled 793,279 TEUs, down 0.6%. PTP contributed approximately 93.3% of their combined 11,767,245 TEUs, with Pasir Gudang supplying 6.7%.

Together with Port Klang, these gateways accounted for approximately 91.7% of the provisional national total. Their concentration of activity makes continued investment and operational resilience nationally important.

Penang remains a gateway for the northern corridor and southern Thailand trade. It handled 987,857 TEUs, down 2.5%, although September recorded growth of 1.4%. Its strategic role extends beyond one period’s softer performance.
Elsewhere, Kuching grew 9.9%, Rajang 9%, Bintulu 4.3% and Sabah 4.1%. Malaysia’s maritime progress includes these regional connections, not only its largest hubs.
From port activity to business value
Daiso’s newly opened RM1.2 billion Global Distribution Centre on Pulau Indah adds another layer to Port Klang’s proposition, serving 27 countries and regions.
Alongside IKEA’s distribution centre on Pulau Indah, it strengthens the connection between maritime access and international distribution.
Elsewhere, Volkswagen’s regional parts distribution centre at PTP demonstrates the wider Malaysian opportunity.
For warehouse operators and logistics providers, the prize is capturing more value around cargo through storage, consolidation, fulfilment and specialist services.
Port Klang’s leadership is therefore more than a ranking. It is a platform for Malaysian enterprise.
For investors and stakeholders, the message is encouraging: the volumes are growing, the capabilities are substantial, and the opportunity reaches well beyond the quay.

Malaysia’s next maritime achievement should be measured not only in containers handled, but in the businesses, careers and possibilities they help carry forward, making Malaysia a nation that moves not just cargo, but people and prosperity too.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
b83436b2b80978cb: Karim Ibrahim’s departure from Malaysia Athletics (MA) should have happened years ago. That it took intervention from World Athletics and a constitutional overhaul to end his presidency says plenty about the federation’s failure to put its own house in order.

The lifetime ban imposed on Karim in 2018 was never lifted. The Court of Arbitration for Sport upheld the findings against him. Yet he returned as MA president in June 2025, relying on a domestic constitutional provision that limited disqualification to five years.
World Athletics continued to regard him as permanently ineligible. MA’s rules, meanwhile, gave him a route back.
That contradiction should never have been allowed to stand.
A national federation cannot claim to represent its sport internationally while maintaining eligibility rules that conflict with those of its international governing body.
World Athletics’ intervention in January this year exposed a failure that MA should have recognised and addressed long before it was forced to do so.
But Karim was not the only person responsible for this episode.
Where were the watchdogs?
MA’s executive council, made up of representatives from its state affiliates, cannot escape scrutiny.
The five-year disqualification provision did not simply find its way into the constitution. It went through the executive council before being put to the affiliates and approved at the AGM.
The very people entrusted with overseeing the federation were part of the process that created the provision allowing Karim to return.

What questions were raised along the way? Did anyone challenge how a domestic five-year disqualification could coexist with a lifetime ban imposed by World Athletics? Did the council consider the consequences for Malaysia’s standing in international athletics?
These are not minor oversights. They go to the heart of what an executive council is supposed to do.
Its members are not there to fill seats, attend meetings or wait for the next overseas competition. They are there to govern, scrutinise decisions and hold the administration accountable.
That means challenging proposals when they threaten the federation’s credibility.
The affiliates cannot now treat the affair as somebody else’s mistake. Their representatives were part of the process, and the provision was approved at their AGM.

An executive council that fails to question decisions of this magnitude is not doing its job. MA needs fewer passengers and more watchdogs – people prepared to challenge the leadership, even when the questions are uncomfortable.
A new rulebook is not enough
The amended constitution is a necessary correction. It is not, by itself, proof that MA has turned a corner.

The federation must now apply its eligibility rules consistently, conduct transparent elections and make its executive council answerable for the decisions it takes. It must also clarify how the new requirements affect its state affiliates.

Karim remains president of the Perak Athletics Association. His disqualification from holding office within MA raises an obvious question about whether he can continue in that state role. MA and Perak must clarify the position rather than leave it to assumption.
But governance is only part of the job. Malaysian athletics has a sporting purpose that has too often been overshadowed by its administrative troubles.
MA must develop athletes, support coaches, strengthen grassroots programmes and build a credible pathway to international competition.
These responsibilities cannot keep taking a back seat while office bearers argue over positions and control.
There is more to being an office bearer than travelling with delegations, attending functions and occupying a seat at meetings. The job is to serve the sport.
The 2027 SEA Games will offer another measure of the country’s ambitions, but the federation’s performance should not be judged by medals alone.
It should also be judged by the quality of the system that produces the athletes and supports those who work with them.
Karim’s exit should be a turning point, not a victory lap for those who remain.
The executive council must examine its own record: the provision it helped put through, the questions it asked or failed to ask, and the consequences that followed.
State affiliates must decide whether their representatives are there to protect the sport or simply occupy positions within its administration.
Karim is gone from the MA presidency. The people who helped create the conditions for his return are still there.
It is time they stopped being passengers.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
4665289b81f88c7a: The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated?  Access to a study's data and code help researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods, and to build on the work.  “Studies involve many choices about how to prepare data, develop models, and evaluate performance. These are sometimes called ‘researcher degrees of freedom,’” says Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. “The choices we make affect the results, and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail.” While sharing code can be a first step, in order for code to be understood and reused, it must be sufficiently structured and described. The problem is that, right now, there is little guidance for researchers on what constitutes a well-organized, well-described collection of code.  This is where an international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute sought to help, by examining how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies. Such studies develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes, such as the risk of developing a disease. Because these models inform decisions about patient care, researchers need to be able to scrutinize how they were built and tested. Using large language models (LLMs), the researchers examined nearly 4,000 papers to identify statements about shared code. They then followed the statements to assess hundreds of associated code repositories. Their review revealed two key gaps: Code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings, recently published in Nature Medicine, are informing TRIPOD-Code, a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share. Following the code TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. To understand current code-sharing practices, the team identified studies citing either guideline. The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models, and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central’s open-access collection.  “The challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent. First, we had to identify whether or not a paper shared code” says Thomas Sounack, the study’s first author. He adds that authors “discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways.” The team used an LLM to help screen papers, identify statements about code availability, and extract links. Software then retrieved the linked repositories — online collections of code and related files — for further assessment. The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed. It also assessed repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse. “The real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text. These models helped us work with information that was scattered across papers and software repositories, rather than neatly organized in a table,” says Pollard, who is a senior author of the study. “That allowed us to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies.” Human reviewers evaluated the work of the LLMs. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results.  Agreement was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Because classification errors remain possible, the authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact. Inconsistent code sharing Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Where code was shared, the contents of repositories varied widely. Some repositories were “extremely well-organized and -documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all,” Sounack says. Good code sharing, he explains, means “giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper.” Practices also varied substantially across journals and countries. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing. The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice. Some researchers, for example, provided synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where the original patient records could not be shared publicly. Setting a standard for code sharing Researchers who share code are already making an effort to make their work transparent. But clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ. TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential. “We want to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code, and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors,” Pollard says. “The review gives us evidence to inform those discussions."

e63fea43dcbf5070: In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.

1be00ca2647ba806: IMDBBy all measures, Rocky (1976) is the most successful sport film of all time. Half a century on from its release, the story of small-time boxer Rocky Balboa – who rises to square up against heavyweight champion Apollo Creed — continues to capture our imagination. Directed by John G. Avildsen, the film won the prestigious Best Picture and Best Directing Oscars in 1977. And the broader franchise, consisting of five sequels and three Creed spin-offs, has generated more than US$1 billion at the global box office. Rocky resonates because it is the ultimate underdog story. The hero is flawed, yet faithful to his dreams – working to overcome his self-doubt. His final victory is not a boxing title, but in proving his worth. Standing your ground The story of Rocky, written by Sylvester Stallone himself, was inspired by a real-life match between heavy weight champion Muhammad Ali and Chuck Wepner. Wepner was a little known boxer from New Jersey at the time. While he didn’t win the fight, he held his own, becoming one of few boxers in history to be able to knock Ali down. As Stallone recalled in an interview: for one brief moment, this supposed stumblebum turned out to be magnificent. And he lasted and knocked the champ down. I thought: ‘if this isn’t a metaphor for life.’ Hollywood lore tells how Stallone wrote the script in just three days after seeing Ali and Wepner’s fight. Stallone later admitted that 90% of this original script was terrible, but the “germ of the idea was there”. He says it took about 25 rewrites to get it right. When interested producers wanted a famous name to take on the eponymous role, Stallone declined. He was determined to play Rocky. It was a big risk, since Stallone was broke – so broke he was forced to sell his dog, Butkus, for US$40. But like Rocky he had faith in himself, and persisted until the studio, United Artists, agreed to cast him in the role. When paid his advance, Stallone was able to buy Butkus back for $15,000. The hound went on to feature in several Rocky films. Butkus, Stallone’s bullmastiff, died in 1981 from a heart attack. IMDB Rocky was filmed on a budget of just US$1 million, a small budget for a film, even in those days. Many of the scenes were shot in public, including those in the famous training montage, in which curious members of the public watch on as Rocky jogs through the streets. In one unscripted moment, a street seller throws Rocky an orange as he jogs past. This detail adds charm to the scene, instilling the sense of Rocky as the everyday man. The training montage also doubles as a metaphor for the American dream, which promises that hard work and persistence will lead to success. Such montages have since become commonplace in sports films, from Karate Kid (1984) to Million Dollar Baby (2004). But Stallone is often credited as having pioneered the format. Rocky represents a powerful ethos There has been much discussion about just what Rocky captured in the American psyche that led to its success. Rocky wasn’t simply a fairytale about the American dream, although this was part of it. The film reflected the neglected working class at a time of growing “ethnic” pride – and local audiences connected with this. The film’s global success, however, arguably comes down to its core message: recognition of the self. As film academic Eric Lichtenfeld argues, Rocky is not just training to become a better boxer – he is searching for respect, both internally and externally. By taking on Apollo Creed, and proving himself to be a worthy opponent, he demonstrates his worth in the world – even if he doesn’t win the final fight. The appeal of this kind of underdog story transcends cultural boundaries. It also goes to the heart of sport, as we’ve seen with Olympians like Eddy the Eagle and Eric the Eel. As Pierre de Courbertin, founder of the Olympics, said: the most important thing […] is not winning, but taking part. The essential thing in life is not conquering but fighting well. Adding to the mystique is the fact that the protagonist’s underdog story is in many ways also Stallone’s story. Rocky was the small-time fighter seizing the opportunity of a lifetime; Stallone was the struggling actor trying to make it big in Hollywood. Rocky’s revival The release of the upcoming film I Play Rocky (2026), a biographical film marking the 50th anniversary, is testament to our enduring fascination with the entwined legends of character and star. Featuring Anthony Ippolito as a young Sylvester Stallone, I Play Rocky portrays the story of how the original film was made. Many of the most beloved elements will return, including the very loyal Butkus, and a recreation of the training montage. The Rocky franchise also continues to grow. Creed IV, the 10th film in the franchise, is currently listed as being in pre-production on IMDB. Lisa J. 540bcf5f777b11b5: China's Xi Jinping places himself firmly in the center of the trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. Doug Mills/Getty ImagesIt was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders. Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine, Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them. But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver? As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School, I saw a lot of style, but less substance. At an eagerly anticipated summit, the leaders of China, Russia and US discussed nuclear weapons – but not much else. What were the key takeaways from the meeting? The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order. And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi. Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president. And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades. A rare airport hug from Xi Jinping. Mandel Ngan/Getty Images It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen. In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds. So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body. And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls. In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985: “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.” All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago, and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter. President Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China’s President Xi Jinping looks on in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026. Iori Sagisawa/AFP via Getty Images What wasn’t discussed? The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations. For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged. But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting. At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi. Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings. British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, U.S. President Franklin Roosevelt and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin sit together at the Yalta Conference. AP Photo This was touted as Yalta II – was it? There were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table. Of course, the big three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years. Also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed. Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary. What Trump may want is detente rather than a new Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that. 82a14710e1b1eacd: A landmark finding of genocide marked a good day for international law. But both the court and the Rohingya minority now need sustained support The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it.
